uni-cse-dbms.title: Database Management Systems (B.Tech CSE)
uni-cse-dbms.description: ER modelling, relational algebra, hands-on SQL with runnable activities, normalization, transactions, indexing and recovery — a complete B.Tech DBMS course with GATE-style unit exams.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Introduction & ER Model
courses.summary: Why databases beat flat files, the three-schema architecture and data independence, and entity–relationship modelling with cardinality, participation, weak entities and ER-to-table mapping.
outcomes: Learners can list the problems of file-based systems that a DBMS solves
Learners can explain logical and physical data independence
Learners can draw an ER model in words with correct cardinality and participation
Learners can convert an ER design into the minimum set of tables

scenes.text: A hostel office keeps student details in five spreadsheets — fees, rooms, mess, library, attendance.
A student changes her phone number; three sheets get updated, two do not. Which number is right?

steps.title: Problems with file systems
steps.body:
- **Redundancy and inconsistency:** the same data stored in many places drifts apart.
- **Difficulty of access:** every new question needs a new program.
- **Isolation:** data scattered in different formats.
- **Integrity problems:** constraints (fee ≥ 0) buried in code.
- **Atomicity problems:** a crash in the middle of a transfer leaves money debited but not credited.
- **Concurrent-access anomalies** and **security** problems.

steps.title: Three-schema architecture
steps.body:
- **External (view) level:** what each user group sees.
- **Conceptual (logical) level:** the whole database's entities, relationships and constraints.
- **Internal (physical) level:** files, indexes, storage.
**Logical data independence:** change the conceptual schema (add a column) without changing external views/apps. **Physical data independence:** change storage (add an index, move files) without changing the conceptual schema. Physical is easier to achieve.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Which independence?
steps.body:
(a) DBA adds a B+ tree index on roll_no → physical.
(b) DBA splits table student into student and address, and redefines the old view so apps still work → logical.
(c) Moving data files to SSD → physical.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Roles and languages
steps.body: DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) defines schema; DML (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) manipulates data; DCL (GRANT, REVOKE) controls access; TCL (COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT) controls transactions. The **DBA** defines schemas, grants rights, tunes and backs up; **end users** run queries/apps.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying logical independence is easier than physical — it is harder.
- Calling a schema an 'instance': the schema is the design; the instance is the data at a moment.
- Listing SELECT as DDL.

activity.prompt: DDL, DML, DCL or TCL?

quiz.q: Adding an index without changing apps shows
quiz.why: Adding an index changes only how data is stored physically, and the applications keep working unchanged. That's physical data independence.

quiz.q: The data stored at a given moment is the
quiz.why: The data stored at a given moment is the database instance, a snapshot. The schema is the design.

quiz.q: Which level describes the whole database for the community of users?
quiz.why: The conceptual (logical) level describes the whole database for all users: its entities, relationships and constraints.

quiz.q: Debit done, credit lost after a crash is a failure of
quiz.why: If the debit happens but the credit is lost, the transaction was only partly done. Atomicity (all or nothing) failed.
GRANT gives access rights, so it's part of DCL (data control language).

scenes.text: A college wants to store students, courses, faculty and who teaches what.
Before any table, the designer sketches entities and relationships — the ER model.

steps.title: ER building blocks
steps.body:
- **Entity / entity set:** a distinguishable thing (Student) — rectangle.
- **Attributes** (ovals): simple vs **composite** (name = first + last), single- vs **multivalued** (phone numbers, double oval), stored vs **derived** (age from DOB, dashed oval), **key attribute** (underlined).
- **Relationship set** (diamond): association among entities; **degree** = number of participating entity sets (binary, ternary).
- **Mapping cardinality:** 1:1, 1:N, N:1, M:N.
- **Participation:** **total** (double line; every entity participates) or **partial**.
- Relationships can have attributes (grade on Enrols).

steps.title: Weak entities and extended ER
steps.body:
A **weak entity** has no key of its own; it is identified by its **owner** entity plus a **partial key (discriminator)** through an **identifying relationship** (double diamond) — with total participation of the weak entity. Example: Dependent(name) owned by Employee.
EER adds **specialisation/generalisation** (ISA) with disjoint/overlapping and total/partial constraints, and **aggregation** (treating a relationship as an entity).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Cardinality from the story
steps.body:
'Each department has exactly one head (a faculty member) and a faculty member heads at most one department.' → Heads is **1:1**; Department participates **totally**, Faculty **partially**.
'A student enrols in many courses and a course has many students' → Enrols is **M:N**, with attribute grade.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Spot the weak entity
steps.body: Loan payments are numbered 1, 2, 3… separately for each loan. Payment has partial key payment_no and is identified by (loan_no, payment_no) → Payment is a **weak entity** owned by Loan.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Making a multivalued attribute a plain column (breaks 1NF later).
- Putting the grade on Student instead of on the Enrols relationship.
- Forgetting that weak entities always participate totally in the identifying relationship.

activity.prompt: Match the ER notation to its meaning

quiz.q: Age computed from date of birth is
quiz.why: Age can be computed from the date of birth, so it's a derived attribute and need not be stored.

quiz.q: A relationship among three entity sets has degree
quiz.why: The degree of a relationship is the number of entity sets it connects. Three entity sets make it ternary (degree 3).

quiz.q: A weak entity is identified by
quiz.why: A weak entity has no key of its own. It's identified by the owner's key plus its own partial key (discriminator).

quiz.q: 'Every loan must belong to a customer' means Loan's participation is
quiz.why: If every loan must belong to a customer, every Loan takes part in the relationship, so its participation is total.
A grade belongs to the pairing of a student with a course, so it's an attribute of the Enrols relationship.

scenes.text: The design is approved; now it must become tables.
Mapping rules decide how many tables are needed and where foreign keys go.

steps.title: Mapping rules
steps.body:
- **Strong entity →** table with its simple attributes; composite attributes flattened; key → primary key.
- **Weak entity →** table with owner's PK + partial key as composite PK; owner's PK also a foreign key.
- **1:N relationship →** add the PK of the '1' side as a foreign key in the 'N' side table (plus relationship attributes). No new table.
- **1:1 →** foreign key on either side — prefer the side with total participation (or merge both into one table if both total).
- **M:N →** new table with both PKs (composite PK) + relationship attributes.
- **Multivalued attribute →** separate table (entity PK, value).
- **n-ary relationship →** new table with all participating PKs.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Minimum tables
steps.body:
Entities Student(roll, name, {phone}), Course(cid, title); Enrols M:N with grade; Department(did) with Belongs (Student N : 1 Department).
- Student(roll, name, did) — FK for 1:N
- StudentPhone(roll, phone) — multivalued
- Course(cid, title)
- Department(did)
- Enrols(roll, cid, grade)
→ **5 tables**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · GATE-style count
steps.body: E1 and E2 linked by a 1:1 relationship R, both with total participation → 1 table (merge). If participation is partial on both, 2 tables (FK on one side, nullable). If R is M:N → 3 tables.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Creating a separate table for every 1:N relationship (not needed).
- Putting the foreign key on the '1' side of a 1:N relationship (would need a list).
- Forgetting the owner key in a weak-entity table.

activity.prompt: Entities A (key a) and B (key b) related by M:N R; A has one multivalued attribute; B is related to entity C by 1:N (C on the N side). Minimum number of tables?

quiz.why: An M:N relationship can't be held by a single foreign key, so it becomes its own table with the keys of both sides.

quiz.q: In 1:N, the foreign key goes in the
quiz.why: In a 1:N relationship each row on the N side points to one row on the 1 side, so the foreign key goes in the N-side table.
A multivalued attribute becomes a separate table with one row for each value, linked by the entity's key.

quiz.q: Weak entity table's primary key is
quiz.why: A weak entity's table has a composite primary key: the owner's primary key plus its partial key.

quiz.q: 1:1 with total participation on both sides can be
quiz.why: When both sides of a 1:1 relationship are total, each row always has a partner, so the two tables can be merged into one.

scenes.text: The college has two Rahul Kumars in the same class.
Name cannot identify a student; roll number can. Keys make every row unique.

steps.title: Kinds of keys
steps.body:
- **Superkey:** any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a tuple.
- **Candidate key:** a minimal superkey (no proper subset is a superkey).
- **Primary key:** the chosen candidate key (NOT NULL, unique). Others are **alternate keys**.
- **Foreign key:** attribute(s) referencing a candidate/primary key of another (or the same) relation.
- **Composite key:** key with more than one attribute; **surrogate key:** system-generated ID.

steps.title: Integrity constraints
steps.body:
- **Domain:** values from the attribute's domain/type, CHECK constraints.
- **Entity integrity:** primary key cannot be NULL.
- **Referential integrity:** a foreign-key value must match an existing referenced key or be NULL. Actions on delete/update: RESTRICT/NO ACTION, CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT.
- **Key constraint:** uniqueness.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Counting superkeys
steps.body:
R(A, B, C, D) with A the only candidate key. Any set containing A is a superkey: the other 3 attributes are free → 2³ = **8 superkeys**.
If A and B are both candidate keys: |contains A| + |contains B| − |contains both| = 8 + 8 − 4 = **12**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Referential actions
steps.body: emp.dept references dept.name with ON DELETE SET NULL. Deleting dept 'HR' sets Meena's and Kabir's dept to NULL. With ON DELETE CASCADE their rows would be deleted. With RESTRICT the delete fails.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling every superkey a candidate key (minimality matters).
- Thinking a foreign key must be NOT NULL — it may be NULL unless declared otherwise.
- Forgetting that a foreign key may reference its own table (emp.mgr → emp.id).

activity.prompt: R(A, B, C, D, E) where A is the only candidate key. How many superkeys?

quiz.why: A minimal superkey, with no unnecessary attribute, is a candidate key.
Entity integrity says a primary key value can't be NULL, since it must identify each row.
If emp.mgr refers to emp.id, it's a foreign key that references its own table: a self-referencing foreign key.

quiz.q: ON DELETE CASCADE on child FK means deleting the parent
quiz.why: With ON DELETE CASCADE, deleting a parent row automatically deletes the child rows that refer to it.

quiz.q: R(A,B,C) with candidate keys A and B: number of superkeys
quiz.why: Superkeys containing A: 2² = 4. Containing B: 4. Containing both A and B: 2. By inclusion–exclusion, 4 + 4 − 2 = 6.

questions.q: Which is NOT a disadvantage of file systems?
questions.why: Data independence is a benefit of a DBMS. File systems suffer from redundancy, integrity problems and concurrent-access anomalies.

questions.q: The design of a database is called its
questions.why: The overall design or structure of a database is its schema.

questions.q: Double rectangle denotes
questions.why: In an ER diagram, a double rectangle denotes a weak entity.

questions.q: Changing indexes without affecting the logical schema is
questions.why: Changing indexes or storage without affecting the logical schema is physical data independence.

questions.q: Each employee works in one department; a department has many employees. Cardinality employee:department =
questions.why: Many employees work in one department, so the employee-to-department cardinality is N:1.

questions.q: PK cannot be NULL is the
questions.why: A primary key can't be NULL is the entity integrity rule. Referential integrity concerns foreign keys.

questions.q: Assertion (A): An M:N relationship needs its own table. Reason (R): Neither side can hold a single foreign key for it. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: an M:N relationship needs its own table. R is true and explains it: neither side can store a single foreign key for it, so a separate table holds the pairs.

questions.q: R(A,B,C,D) with candidate keys AB and C: number of superkeys
questions.why: Superkeys containing AB: 2² = 4. Containing C: 2³ = 8. Containing both AB and C: 2 (D free). So 4 + 8 − 2 = 10.

questions.q: Weak entity Dependent(name, age) of Employee(eid). Primary key of Dependent table:
questions.why: A weak entity's table uses the owner's key plus its partial key, so the key of Dependent is (eid, name).

questions.q: Case: a hospital stores patients' multiple phone numbers in one comma-separated column. The proper design is
questions.why: Phone numbers are multivalued, so they should be in their own PatientPhone table, one row per number. A comma-separated column breaks atomicity.

questions.q: Entities E1, E2, E3; R1 (E1–E2) is 1:N, R2 (E2–E3) is M:N, E3 has a multivalued attribute. Minimum tables:
questions.why: Tables: E1; E2 (with an FK for the 1:N relationship); E3; R2 for the M:N relationship; and a table for E3's multivalued attribute. That's 5.

questions.q: Which referential action could silently delete many rows?
questions.why: CASCADE deletes child rows when the parent is deleted, and this can chain through further levels, so it can silently remove many rows.

questions.q: Logical data independence is harder than physical because
options: apps depend directly on logical structure
questions.why: Logical independence is harder because applications depend directly on the logical structure, so changes to it must be hidden by views.

questions.q: A ternary relationship among Supplier, Part, Project maps to a table with
options: three FKs forming the key (in general)
questions.why: A ternary relationship becomes a table holding the primary keys of all three participants as foreign keys, which together generally form the key.

questions.q: In R(A,B,C,D,E), if every superkey must contain A and B and AB is a key, the number of superkeys is
questions.why: Every superkey must contain A and B, so only C, D and E can vary freely: 2³ = 8 superkeys.

questions.q: 1:1 relationship, total participation of E1 only. Best mapping:
options: FK in E1 referencing E2 (NOT NULL)
questions.why: For a 1:1 relationship where only E1 is total, put the foreign key in E1 referencing E2 and make it NOT NULL, because every E1 row has a partner.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Relational Model, Algebra & Calculus
courses.summary: Relations, tuples and domains; the relational-algebra operators (select, project, union, difference, product, rename, joins, intersection, division) and tuple/domain relational calculus, with query-writing and tuple-count problems.
outcomes: Learners can write relational-algebra queries for typical questions
Learners can compute result sizes of products and joins
Learners can express 'for all' queries with division
Learners can translate between algebra, calculus and SQL

scenes.text: An admissions office has a list of 10,000 applicants.
First keep only those from Kerala with ≥ 90% (select), then show only names and phones (project).

steps.title: Relations and the six basic operators
steps.body:
A **relation** is a set of tuples over attributes with domains; order of tuples/attributes does not matter; no duplicate tuples. Degree = number of attributes; cardinality = number of tuples.
- **σ (select):** rows satisfying a predicate, σ_{salary>50000}(emp).
- **π (project):** chosen columns, duplicates removed, π_{name}(emp).
- **∪, −:** union and set difference (need union-compatible relations: same degree and domains).
- **× (Cartesian product):** every pair of tuples; |R × S| = |R|·|S|, degree adds.
- **ρ (rename).**
Derived: ∩ = R − (R − S), joins, division.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Write the query
steps.body:
Names of IT employees earning above 50000:
π_{name}(σ_{dept='IT' ∧ salary>50000}(emp)) → {Asha, Ravi}.
SQL equivalent: `SELECT DISTINCT name FROM emp WHERE dept='IT' AND salary>50000;` (DISTINCT because algebra uses sets).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Sizes
steps.body:
R has 5 tuples and 3 attributes, S has 4 tuples and 2 attributes.
- R × S: **20 tuples, degree 5**.
- π over a non-key attribute of R: between 1 and 5 tuples.
- σ: between 0 and 5 tuples.
- If R, S union-compatible with |R| = 5, |S| = 4: |R ∪ S| ∈ [5, 9], |R − S| ∈ [1, 5], |R ∩ S| ∈ [0, 4].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting π removes duplicates.
- Taking a union of relations with different schemas.
- Applying σ after π that removed the attribute used in the condition.

activity.prompt: Match the operator
pairs: Pairs every tuple of R with every tuple of S
Tuples in R but not in S

quiz.why: The Cartesian product pairs every tuple of R with every tuple of S: 6 × 7 = 42.
Union, intersection and difference need the two relations to be union compatible: the same number of attributes with matching domains.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a basic operator?
quiz.why: Natural join isn't a basic operator, since it can be built from product, selection and projection. The basic ones are σ, π, ∪, − and ×.
R ∩ S = R − (R − S): remove from R the part not in S, and what remains is the common part.
R − S has at most |R| tuples, and exactly 10 if R and S have no tuples in common.

scenes.text: One table has students with hostel IDs; another has hostels with wardens.
A join pairs each student with the warden of their hostel.

steps.title: Join family
steps.body:
- **Theta join** R ⋈_θ S = σ_θ(R × S). **Equi-join** when θ uses only =.
- **Natural join** R ⋈ S: equi-join on all common attribute names, keeping one copy of each.
- **Outer joins:** left (⟕), right (⟖), full (⟗) keep unmatched tuples padded with NULL.
- **Semi-join** R ⋉ S: tuples of R that have a match in S (only R's attributes).
Size of natural join: if no common attributes → |R|·|S|; if the common attribute is a key of S and a foreign key in R (NOT NULL) → exactly |R|.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · emp ⋈ dept
steps.body: Joining emp.dept = dept.name gives 6 tuples (each employee matches one department). A left outer join dept ⟕ emp gives 7 tuples: the 6 matches plus (Legal, Chennai, NULL…) because Legal has no employees.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Bounds
steps.body:
R(A, B) has 100 tuples, S(B, C) has 50 tuples.
- Min |R ⋈ S| = 0 (no matching B), max = 100 × 50 = 5000 (all share one B value).
- If B is the primary key of S and R.B is a NOT NULL foreign key → exactly **100**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking natural join with no common attributes is empty — it becomes a Cartesian product.
- Forgetting outer joins add NULL-padded tuples.
- Joining on attributes that only coincidentally share a name.

activity.prompt: R(A,B) has 40 tuples and S(B,C) has 25 tuples; B is the key of S and R.B is a non-null foreign key to S. How many tuples in R ⋈ S?

quiz.q: Natural join of relations with no common attributes equals
quiz.why: With no common attributes, a natural join has nothing to match on, so every tuple pairs with every other. That is the Cartesian product.
A left outer join keeps all tuples of the left relation, padding the unmatched ones with NULLs.
A θ-join is a selection σ_θ applied to the Cartesian product R × S.
The largest possible join result happens if every tuple matches every tuple (all common values equal): 10 × 20 = 200.

quiz.q: dept ⟕ emp here returns how many tuples?
quiz.why: Every employee matches a department (6 rows), and the left outer join also keeps Legal, which has no employees: 6 + 1 = 7.

scenes.text: The lab coordinator wants students who completed *all* five experiments.
'For all' questions call for division.

steps.title: Division
steps.body:
For R(A, B) and S(B): R ÷ S = the A-values that are paired in R with **every** B-value in S.
In basic operators: R ÷ S = π_A(R) − π_A((π_A(R) × S) − R).
Intuition: (π_A(R) × S) lists every pair that *should* exist; subtracting R leaves missing pairs; their A-values are disqualified.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Division by hand
steps.body:
Done(student, exp): (Anu, E1), (Anu, E2), (Bala, E1), (Chitra, E1), (Chitra, E2), (Chitra, E3). Exps(exp) = {E1, E2}.
- π_student(Done) × Exps = all 6 pairs for Anu, Bala, Chitra with E1, E2.
- Minus Done → missing (Bala, E2).
- Disqualified: Bala. Result: **{Anu, Chitra}**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · A typical query
steps.body: Employees who earn more than every Sales employee — using algebra: emp1 := ρ_{e1}(emp), sales := σ_{dept='Sales'}(emp). Employees NOT qualifying are those with some Sales salary ≥ theirs: π_{e1.name}(σ_{e1.salary ≤ s.salary}(emp1 × ρ_s(sales))). Answer = π_name(emp) − that set → {Asha, Ravi} (Zoya is ≤ her own 55000).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using division where 'at least one' is asked (that's just a join).
- Forgetting union compatibility in the subtraction step.
- Confusing 'more than every' (needs set difference/division) with 'more than some' (a join suffices).

activity.prompt: Arrange the steps to compute R(A,B) ÷ S(B)
items: Subtract R to get missing pairs
Project the missing pairs on A

quiz.why: Division answers 'for all' questions, such as employees who worked on all projects.

quiz.q: If S is empty, R ÷ S is
quiz.why: If S is empty, every A value in R vacuously pairs with 'all' of S, so R ÷ S is the projection of R on A.

quiz.q: 'Employees who work on at least one project' needs
quiz.why: 'At least one' is existential, so it needs a join or semi-join, not division.

quiz.q: In the example, Bala is excluded because
quiz.why: For Bala to qualify he'd have to appear with every required value. The pair (Bala, E2) is missing, so he's excluded.

options: A (attributes of R not in S)
quiz.why: R ÷ S has the attributes of R that aren't in S, here A.

scenes.text: Algebra says *how* to get the answer (procedural). Calculus says *what* the answer is (declarative).
SQL borrowed its declarative style from calculus.

steps.title: Tuple and domain calculus
steps.body:
- **Tuple relational calculus (TRC):** { t | P(t) }, e.g. { t.name | t ∈ emp ∧ t.salary > 50000 }.
- **Domain relational calculus (DRC):** variables range over attribute values, e.g. { ⟨n⟩ | ∃i, d, s, m (⟨i, n, d, s, m⟩ ∈ emp ∧ s > 50000) }.
- Quantifiers ∃ (exists) and ∀ (for all).
- **Safe expressions** guarantee finite results (e.g. { t | ¬(t ∈ emp) } is unsafe — infinite).
- **Codd's theorem:** relational algebra and safe relational calculus are equally expressive (**relationally complete**).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Translate to TRC
steps.body:
Names of employees who work in a department located in Delhi:
{ t.name | t ∈ emp ∧ ∃d (d ∈ dept ∧ d.name = t.dept ∧ d.city = 'Delhi') } → {Meena, Kabir}.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · For-all in TRC
steps.body:
Students who did every experiment:
{ s.student | s ∈ Done ∧ ∀e (e ∈ Exps → ∃d (d ∈ Done ∧ d.student = s.student ∧ d.exp = e.exp)) }. Same result as division: {Anu, Chitra}.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing unsafe negations without restricting the variable to a relation.
- Forgetting the implication form for ∀ (∀e (e ∈ S → …)).
- Claiming SQL is exactly calculus — SQL adds bags (duplicates), aggregates, NULLs.

statements.why: It specifies a sequence of operations.

statements.s: { t | ¬(t ∈ R) } is a safe expression.
Safe TRC and relational algebra have the same expressive power.
SQL works strictly on sets without duplicates.

quiz.why: In tuple relational calculus, variables range over tuples (rows).
A query language is relationally complete if it's at least as expressive as relational algebra (Codd's notion).
A universal quantifier ∀x is normally paired with implication: ∀x (x ∈ S → …), meaning every x in S satisfies the condition.
Relational calculus is declarative: it says what to retrieve, not how. Algebra specifies the steps.
Unsafe calculus expressions, such as the set of all tuples not in a relation, could produce infinite results.

questions.q: A tuple is a
questions.why: A tuple is a row of a relation.

questions.q: π removes
questions.why: In relational algebra, projection (π) works on sets, so it removes duplicate rows from the result.

questions.q: Number of attributes is the
questions.why: The number of attributes of a relation is its degree. The number of tuples is its cardinality.

questions.q: R has 3 attributes, S has 4: degree of R × S
questions.why: The product has all the attributes of both relations, so the degree is 3 + 4 = 7.

questions.q: Natural join uses
questions.why: A natural join matches on all attributes that have the same name in both relations.

questions.q: Division is used for
questions.why: Division is used for 'for all' queries.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Intersection is not a basic operator. Reason (R): R ∩ S = R − (R − S). Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: intersection isn't basic. R is true and explains it: R ∩ S = R − (R − S), so it can be built from difference.

questions.q: |R| = 8, |S| = 5, union-compatible. Range of |R ∪ S|:
questions.why: The union has at least 8 tuples (if S ⊆ R) and at most 8 + 5 = 13 (if disjoint). So between 8 and 13.

questions.q: Result of σ_{salary>100000}(emp) on our emp table
questions.why: The highest salary in the table is 90,000, so no row has salary above 100,000 and the result is empty.

questions.q: Case: list departments with no employees using algebra.
questions.why: Departments with no employees = all department names minus those that appear in emp: π_name(dept) − π_dept(emp). That gives Legal.
Values 1 and 3 each pair with both x and y in R, while 2 pairs only with x. So R ÷ S = {1, 3}.

questions.q: R(A,B) 200 tuples; S(B,C) 300 tuples; B is the key of S, R.B a non-null FK. |R ⋈ S| =
questions.why: B is the key of S and R.B is a non-null foreign key, so each R tuple matches exactly one S tuple. The join has 200 tuples.

questions.q: Which pair of expressions is equivalent?
options: R × S and R ⋈ S always
questions.why: Cascaded selections combine: σ_c1(σ_c2(R)) = σ_{c1∧c2}(R). Projection doesn't distribute over difference, and the other pairs aren't equal.

questions.q: { t | t ∈ emp ∧ ¬∃u (u ∈ emp ∧ u.salary > t.salary) } returns
questions.why: The formula selects employees for whom no other employee has a higher salary, which gives the highest-paid employee(s).

questions.q: Full outer join of R (5 tuples) and S (4 tuples) where exactly 3 R tuples match exactly one S tuple each (distinct): size
questions.why: 3 R tuples match 3 S tuples, giving 3 rows. The 2 unmatched R tuples and the 1 unmatched S tuple each give a padded row: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.

questions.q: Relational algebra cannot directly express
questions.why: Relational algebra can't express transitive closure (recursion of arbitrary depth). Recursive SQL, with WITH RECURSIVE, extends it.

courses.title: Unit 3 · SQL I — DDL, DML, Queries & Aggregates
courses.summary: Hands-on SQL: creating tables with constraints, inserting/updating/deleting, SELECT with WHERE, ORDER BY, LIKE, BETWEEN, IN, NULL handling, aggregates, GROUP BY and HAVING — with runnable code activities.
outcomes: Learners can create tables with keys and constraints
Learners can write filtered and sorted queries
Learners can use aggregates with GROUP BY and HAVING correctly
Learners can reason about NULLs in conditions and aggregates

scenes.text: A startup's HR team needs tables for departments and employees.
They want the database itself to refuse bad data — negative salaries, unknown departments.

steps.title: CREATE TABLE with constraints
steps.body:
`CREATE TABLE emp (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  dept TEXT REFERENCES dept(name) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  salary INTEGER CHECK (salary >= 0),
  email TEXT UNIQUE,
  mgr INTEGER REFERENCES emp(id)
);`
Other DDL: `ALTER TABLE emp ADD COLUMN phone TEXT;` `DROP TABLE t;` `TRUNCATE` (remove all rows, keep structure; not in every dialect).

steps.title: Running example
steps.body: Tables: **dept(name, city)** — IT/Pune, HR/Delhi, Sales/Mumbai, Legal/Chennai. **emp(id, name, dept, salary, mgr)** — 1 Asha IT 90000 NULL · 2 Ravi IT 60000 1 · 3 Meena HR 50000 1 · 4 Kabir HR 45000 3 · 5 Zoya Sales 55000 1 · 6 Dev Sales 40000 5.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Which inserts fail?
steps.body:
With the constraints above:
- `INSERT INTO emp VALUES (7,'Ira','IT',-5,NULL,1);` → **fails CHECK** (salary < 0).
- `INSERT INTO emp VALUES (2,'Om','IT',30000,NULL,1);` → **fails PRIMARY KEY** (id 2 exists).
- `INSERT INTO emp VALUES (8,'Om','Design',30000,NULL,1);` → **fails FOREIGN KEY** if enforcement is on (no dept 'Design').
- `INSERT INTO emp VALUES (9,'Om',NULL,30000,NULL,1);` → succeeds (FK may be NULL).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP
steps.body: DELETE FROM emp WHERE dept='HR' → removes 2 rows, can be rolled back, fires triggers. TRUNCATE (where supported) → removes all rows quickly. DROP TABLE emp → removes the table itself.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that SQLite enforces foreign keys only when `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`.
- Using `= NULL` instead of `IS NULL`.
- Assuming UNIQUE forbids multiple NULLs — most systems allow many NULLs in a UNIQUE column.

activity.prompt: Create a table course(code TEXT PRIMARY KEY, credits INTEGER CHECK(credits BETWEEN 1 AND 6)), insert ('CS201', 4) and ('CS202', 3), then select all rows ordered by code.
activity.starter: -- write CREATE TABLE, two INSERTs and a SELECT
activity.hint: Separate statements with semicolons.

quiz.why: A CHECK (salary >= 0) constraint rejects negative values. The other constraints don't check the value range.
A foreign key may be NULL unless it's declared NOT NULL, since NULL means 'no reference'.

quiz.q: Which statement removes the table definition?
quiz.why: DROP TABLE removes the whole table, its definition and data. DELETE removes rows only.
ALTER TABLE changes the schema, so it's a DDL statement.
A comparison with NULL using = never gives true, so use IS NULL (or IS NOT NULL).

scenes.text: Who earns more than ₹50,000? Who has a name starting with 'K'? Who has no manager?
Each question is one short SELECT.

steps.title: Query skeleton
steps.body:
`SELECT [DISTINCT] columns FROM table WHERE condition ORDER BY col [ASC|DESC] LIMIT n;`
Logical order of evaluation: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.
Operators: =, <>, <, >, BETWEEN a AND b (inclusive), IN (…), LIKE ('K%' starts with K, '_a%' second letter a), IS NULL, AND/OR/NOT.

steps.title: Data
steps.body: Tables: **dept(name, city)** — IT/Pune, HR/Delhi, Sales/Mumbai, Legal/Chennai. **emp(id, name, dept, salary, mgr)** — 1 Asha IT 90000 NULL · 2 Ravi IT 60000 1 · 3 Meena HR 50000 1 · 4 Kabir HR 45000 3 · 5 Zoya Sales 55000 1 · 6 Dev Sales 40000 5.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Filters
steps.body:
- `SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary BETWEEN 45000 AND 55000 ORDER BY name;` → Kabir, Meena, Zoya.
- `SELECT name FROM emp WHERE name LIKE '_a%';` → Kabir, Ravi (second letter 'a').
- `SELECT name FROM emp WHERE mgr IS NULL;` → Asha.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · NULL logic
steps.body: `SELECT name FROM emp WHERE mgr <> 1;` returns Kabir (mgr 3) and Dev (mgr 5) — **not Asha**, because NULL <> 1 is UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE rows. To include her: `WHERE mgr <> 1 OR mgr IS NULL`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a column alias from SELECT inside WHERE (WHERE runs first).
- Forgetting that BETWEEN is inclusive.
- Expecting NOT IN (subquery) to work when the subquery returns a NULL — it returns no rows.

activity.prompt: List the names of employees earning more than 50000, highest salary first.
activity.solution: SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary > 50000 ORDER BY salary DESC;
activity.hint: ORDER BY salary DESC puts the biggest first.
activity.setup: CREATE TABLE dept(name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, city TEXT);INSERT INTO dept VALUES ('IT','Pune'),('HR','Delhi'),('Sales','Mumbai'),('Legal','Chennai');CREATE TABLE emp(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept TEXT REFERENCES dept(name), salary INTEGER, mgr INTEGER);INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Asha','IT',90000,NULL),(2,'Ravi','IT',60000,1),(3,'Meena','HR',50000,1),(4,'Kabir','HR',45000,3),(5,'Zoya','Sales',55000,1),(6,'Dev','Sales',40000,5);

quiz.why: In LIKE, % stands for any sequence of characters, so 'S%' matches names beginning with S.

quiz.q: WHERE runs ___ SELECT in logical order
quiz.why: Logically, FROM and WHERE are evaluated first, then grouping, HAVING, and finally SELECT. So WHERE runs before SELECT.
BETWEEN is inclusive of both ends, so 20 is included.

quiz.q: `WHERE mgr <> 1` on Asha (mgr NULL) evaluates to
quiz.why: NULL <> 1 is UNKNOWN (not true), so WHERE doesn't keep Asha's row. SQL uses three-valued logic.
DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result.

scenes.text: Finance asks: total payroll per department, and which departments spend more than ₹1 lakh.
Group rows by department, then filter the groups.

steps.title: Aggregates
steps.body:
COUNT(*), COUNT(col) (ignores NULLs), SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. Aggregates ignore NULLs (except COUNT(*)).
`SELECT dept, COUNT(*), AVG(salary) FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;`
- **WHERE** filters rows *before* grouping; **HAVING** filters groups *after*.
- Every non-aggregated SELECT column must appear in GROUP BY (standard SQL).

steps.title: Data
steps.body: Tables: **dept(name, city)** — IT/Pune, HR/Delhi, Sales/Mumbai, Legal/Chennai. **emp(id, name, dept, salary, mgr)** — 1 Asha IT 90000 NULL · 2 Ravi IT 60000 1 · 3 Meena HR 50000 1 · 4 Kabir HR 45000 3 · 5 Zoya Sales 55000 1 · 6 Dev Sales 40000 5.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Group totals
steps.body:
`SELECT dept, SUM(salary) FROM emp GROUP BY dept;` → HR 95000, IT 150000, Sales 95000.
`… HAVING SUM(salary) > 100000` → only IT.
`SELECT dept, AVG(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary > 45000 GROUP BY dept;` → HR 50000 (Kabir filtered out first), IT 75000, Sales 55000.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · COUNT and NULL
steps.body: `SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(mgr) FROM emp;` → 6 and 5 (Asha's NULL mgr not counted). `SELECT AVG(mgr)` would average only 5 values.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting an aggregate condition in WHERE (`WHERE SUM(salary) > …` is an error).
- Selecting `name` with GROUP BY dept (non-grouped column).
- Assuming AVG treats NULL as 0.

activity.prompt: For each department show dept and the maximum salary, ordered by dept name. Output columns: dept, max salary.
activity.solution: SELECT dept, MAX(salary) FROM emp GROUP BY dept ORDER BY dept;
activity.hint: GROUP BY dept, then ORDER BY dept.
activity.setup: CREATE TABLE dept(name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, city TEXT);INSERT INTO dept VALUES ('IT','Pune'),('HR','Delhi'),('Sales','Mumbai'),('Legal','Chennai');CREATE TABLE emp(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept TEXT REFERENCES dept(name), salary INTEGER, mgr INTEGER);INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Asha','IT',90000,NULL),(2,'Ravi','IT',60000,1),(3,'Meena','HR',50000,1),(4,'Kabir','HR',45000,3),(5,'Zoya','Sales',55000,1),(6,'Dev','Sales',40000,5);

quiz.why: HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY. WHERE filters individual rows before grouping.
COUNT(column) skips NULLs. COUNT(*) counts all rows.

quiz.q: SUM(salary) for Sales in our data
quiz.why: The Sales department's salaries add up to 55,000 + 40,000 = 95,000.

quiz.q: Which is invalid in standard SQL?
options: SELECT name, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept
SELECT dept FROM emp GROUP BY dept
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept
quiz.why: In standard SQL, every selected column must be grouped or aggregated. name is neither, so that query is invalid.
AVG ignores NULLs: (10 + 20)/2 = 15, not (10 + 20)/3.

scenes.text: HR gives every HR employee a 10% raise and wants a 'band' label for each salary.
UPDATE changes data; CASE builds computed labels.

steps.title: DML statements
steps.body:
- `INSERT INTO t (cols) VALUES (…), (…);` or `INSERT INTO t SELECT …;`
- `UPDATE t SET col = expr WHERE condition;` — without WHERE, every row changes!
- `DELETE FROM t WHERE condition;`
- **CASE:** `CASE WHEN salary >= 60000 THEN 'High' WHEN salary >= 50000 THEN 'Mid' ELSE 'Entry' END`.

steps.title: Data
steps.body: Tables: **dept(name, city)** — IT/Pune, HR/Delhi, Sales/Mumbai, Legal/Chennai. **emp(id, name, dept, salary, mgr)** — 1 Asha IT 90000 NULL · 2 Ravi IT 60000 1 · 3 Meena HR 50000 1 · 4 Kabir HR 45000 3 · 5 Zoya Sales 55000 1 · 6 Dev Sales 40000 5.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Raise
steps.body: `UPDATE emp SET salary = salary + salary / 10 WHERE dept = 'HR';` → Meena 55000, Kabir 49500 (integer arithmetic avoids floating-point surprises like 49500.00000000001).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Banding
steps.body: `SELECT name, CASE WHEN salary >= 60000 THEN 'High' WHEN salary >= 50000 THEN 'Mid' ELSE 'Entry' END AS band FROM emp ORDER BY id;` → Asha High, Ravi High, Meena Mid, Kabir Entry, Zoya Mid, Dev Entry. CASE checks conditions top-down and stops at the first TRUE.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Running UPDATE/DELETE without WHERE.
- Ordering CASE branches wrongly (put the most restrictive condition first).
- Updating a primary key that other rows reference.

activity.prompt: Give every HR employee a 10% raise (use salary + salary/10), then list HR names and salaries ordered by name.
activity.starter: -- UPDATE first, then SELECT
activity.solution:
UPDATE emp SET salary = salary + salary / 10 WHERE dept = 'HR';
SELECT name, salary FROM emp WHERE dept = 'HR' ORDER BY name;
activity.hint: Two statements separated by a semicolon.
activity.setup: CREATE TABLE dept(name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, city TEXT);INSERT INTO dept VALUES ('IT','Pune'),('HR','Delhi'),('Sales','Mumbai'),('Legal','Chennai');CREATE TABLE emp(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept TEXT REFERENCES dept(name), salary INTEGER, mgr INTEGER);INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Asha','IT',90000,NULL),(2,'Ravi','IT',60000,1),(3,'Meena','HR',50000,1),(4,'Kabir','HR',45000,3),(5,'Zoya','Sales',55000,1),(6,'Dev','Sales',40000,5);

quiz.why: UPDATE without WHERE changes every row in the table, which is a common and dangerous mistake.
Top-down.

options: copy query results into a table
quiz.why: INSERT … SELECT inserts the rows returned by a query into a table, copying data in bulk.

quiz.q: Band for Zoya (55000) in the example
quiz.why: Zoya earns 55,000, which is at least 50,000 but below 60,000, so she falls in the 'Mid' band.

quiz.q: DELETE FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT' removes
quiz.why: There are two employees in IT (Asha and Ravi), so DELETE removes 2 rows.

questions.q: Which clause filters groups?
questions.why: HAVING filters groups after aggregation. WHERE filters rows before it.

questions.q: Which is DDL?
questions.why: CREATE defines schema objects, so it is DDL. INSERT, UPDATE and SELECT are DML.

questions.q: COUNT(*) counts
questions.why: COUNT(*) counts all the rows, including those with NULLs.

questions.q: `LIKE '%a'` matches
questions.why: LIKE '%a' matches any string that ends with a, since % covers whatever comes before.

questions.q: Logical order: which runs first?
questions.why: In logical order, WHERE is applied right after FROM, before grouping, HAVING, SELECT and ORDER BY.

questions.q: AVG(salary) over our emp table ≈
questions.why: The salaries total 340,000 over 6 employees, so the average is 340,000/6 ≈ 56,667.

questions.q: Assertion (A): `WHERE COUNT(*) > 1` is invalid. Reason (R): WHERE is evaluated before grouping. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: aggregates like COUNT(*) can't be used in WHERE. R is true and explains it: WHERE is evaluated before grouping, so no aggregate exists yet. Use HAVING.

questions.q: `SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp WHERE salary > 50000 GROUP BY dept;` returns
questions.why: The rows with salary above 50,000 are Asha and Ravi (IT) and Zoya (Sales). Grouping gives IT 2 and Sales 1.

questions.q: `SELECT name FROM emp WHERE mgr IN (1, 3) ORDER BY name;`
questions.why: Managers 1 and 3 supervise Ravi, Meena and Zoya (mgr 1) and Kabir (mgr 3). Sorted: Kabir, Meena, Ravi, Zoya.

questions.q: Case: a report shows department average salaries but HR looks too low because one HR employee's salary is NULL. What does AVG do with it?
questions.why: AVG skips NULLs, so the HR average is computed from the non-NULL salaries only. It doesn't treat NULL as 0.

questions.q: `SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT dept) FROM emp;`
questions.why: COUNT(DISTINCT dept) counts different department names: IT, HR and Sales, which makes 3.

questions.q: `SELECT dept FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING MIN(salary) >= 45000;`
questions.why: The group minimums are HR 45,000, IT 60,000 and Sales 40,000. Only HR and IT are at least 45,000.

questions.q: `SELECT name FROM emp WHERE NOT (mgr = 1);`
questions.why: NOT (mgr = 1) is true for rows where mgr is a different non-NULL value, Kabir and Dev. For Asha, mgr is NULL, so mgr = 1 is UNKNOWN and NOT UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN, so she's excluded.

questions.q: After `UPDATE emp SET salary = salary * 2 WHERE salary < 50000;` total payroll becomes
questions.why: Only Kabir (45,000) and Dev (40,000) are under 50,000, and doubling them adds 85,000. The total becomes 340,000 + 85,000 = 425,000.

questions.q: `SELECT dept, SUM(salary) s FROM emp GROUP BY dept ORDER BY s DESC LIMIT 1;`
questions.why: The total salaries are IT 150,000, HR 95,000 and Sales 95,000. Ordered descending, the top one is IT 150,000.

questions.q: UNIQUE column with two NULL values in SQLite/PostgreSQL:
questions.why: A UNIQUE column in SQLite and PostgreSQL allows several NULLs, because NULLs aren't considered equal to each other.

courses.title: Unit 4 · SQL II — Joins, Subqueries, Views & Window Functions
courses.summary: Inner, outer and self joins; scalar, IN, EXISTS and correlated subqueries; ANY/ALL; set operations; views; the nth-highest-salary family of problems; window functions; plus triggers, indexes and SQL transactions — each with runnable SQL.
outcomes: Learners can choose the right join for a question
Learners can write correlated and EXISTS subqueries
Learners can use UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT and views
Learners can solve ranking problems with subqueries and window functions

scenes.text: The travel desk needs each employee's office city, and the facilities team wants offices that have nobody yet.
HR also wants every employee next to their manager's name.

steps.title: Join syntax
steps.body:
- `SELECT e.name, d.city FROM emp e JOIN dept d ON e.dept = d.name;` (INNER)
- `FROM dept d LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.dept = d.name` keeps every department (NULLs when no employee).
- RIGHT and FULL OUTER JOIN exist in most systems (SQLite added them in version 3.39).
- **Self join:** `FROM emp e JOIN emp m ON e.mgr = m.id` pairs employees with managers.
- **CROSS JOIN:** Cartesian product.

steps.title: Data
steps.body: Tables: **dept(name, city)** — IT/Pune, HR/Delhi, Sales/Mumbai, Legal/Chennai. **emp(id, name, dept, salary, mgr)** — 1 Asha IT 90000 NULL · 2 Ravi IT 60000 1 · 3 Meena HR 50000 1 · 4 Kabir HR 45000 3 · 5 Zoya Sales 55000 1 · 6 Dev Sales 40000 5.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Manager names
steps.body: `SELECT e.name, m.name AS manager FROM emp e JOIN emp m ON e.mgr = m.id ORDER BY e.id;` → Ravi–Asha, Meena–Asha, Kabir–Meena, Zoya–Asha, Dev–Zoya. Asha disappears in an inner join (mgr NULL); use LEFT JOIN to keep her with manager NULL.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Empty departments
steps.body: `SELECT d.name FROM dept d LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.dept = d.name WHERE e.id IS NULL;` → **Legal**. The WHERE on the right table's key finds unmatched rows (an 'anti-join').

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting a right-table filter in WHERE after a LEFT JOIN — it silently turns it into an inner join; put such filters in ON.
- Forgetting table aliases in self joins.
- Omitting the join condition (accidental Cartesian product).

activity.prompt: Show name and city of employees whose department is located in Delhi, ordered by name.
activity.starter:
SELECT e.name, d.city
FROM emp e JOIN dept d ON e.dept = d.name
-- filter and order
;
activity.solution: SELECT e.name, d.city FROM emp e JOIN dept d ON e.dept = d.name WHERE d.city = 'Delhi' ORDER BY e.name;
activity.hint: Filter on d.city.

quiz.q: Which join keeps all rows of the left table?
quiz.why: A LEFT OUTER JOIN keeps all the rows of the left table, filling in NULLs where there's no match.

quiz.q: A self join joins a table with
quiz.why: A self join joins a table with itself, using two aliases, such as an employee with their manager.

quiz.q: Inner join of emp with emp (mgr = id) returns how many rows here?
quiz.why: Asha has no manager (NULL), so she doesn't match anything in the inner join. The other 5 employees do, giving 5 rows.
Without an ON condition (or WHERE) joining the tables, every row is paired with every row, giving a Cartesian product.

quiz.q: A WHERE filter on the right table after LEFT JOIN may
options: turn it into an inner join
quiz.why: After a LEFT JOIN, unmatched rows have NULLs for the right table. A WHERE condition on a right-table column fails for them, so they vanish and the query acts like an inner join.

scenes.text: Leadership asks: who earns more than the company average? who earns the most in their own department?
Queries inside queries answer these.

steps.title: Kinds of subqueries
steps.body:
- **Scalar:** returns one value: `WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp)`.
- **IN / NOT IN:** membership in a set.
- **EXISTS / NOT EXISTS:** true if the subquery returns any row; NULL-safe for anti-joins.
- **Correlated:** refers to the outer row and is (logically) re-evaluated per row: `WHERE salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp e2 WHERE e2.dept = e1.dept)`.
- **ANY / ALL:** `salary > ALL (SELECT salary FROM emp WHERE dept='Sales')` (not in SQLite; use MAX instead).

steps.title: Data
steps.body: Tables: **dept(name, city)** — IT/Pune, HR/Delhi, Sales/Mumbai, Legal/Chennai. **emp(id, name, dept, salary, mgr)** — 1 Asha IT 90000 NULL · 2 Ravi IT 60000 1 · 3 Meena HR 50000 1 · 4 Kabir HR 45000 3 · 5 Zoya Sales 55000 1 · 6 Dev Sales 40000 5.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Department toppers
steps.body: `SELECT name, dept FROM emp e1 WHERE salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp e2 WHERE e2.dept = e1.dept);` → Asha (IT), Meena (HR), Zoya (Sales).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Managers via EXISTS
steps.body: `SELECT name FROM emp m WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM emp e WHERE e.mgr = m.id);` → Asha, Meena, Zoya (they manage someone). The NOT EXISTS version returns Ravi, Kabir, Dev.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- `NOT IN (SELECT mgr FROM emp)` returns **no rows** because the list contains NULL (Asha's mgr). Use NOT EXISTS or filter `WHERE mgr IS NOT NULL`.
- Using `=` with a subquery that can return several rows.
- Forgetting the correlation condition, which turns a correlated query into a global one.

activity.prompt: List names of employees who earn more than the average salary of all employees, ordered by name.
activity.solution: SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp) ORDER BY name;
activity.hint: Average is about 56667.

quiz.q: EXISTS returns true when the subquery
quiz.why: EXISTS is true if the subquery returns at least one row, whatever its values.

quiz.q: Why does `id NOT IN (SELECT mgr FROM emp)` return nothing?
quiz.why: NOT IN with a list that contains NULL can never be TRUE, because x <> NULL is UNKNOWN. So no rows come back. Use NOT EXISTS or filter out the NULLs.

options: a column of the outer query
quiz.why: A correlated subquery uses a column from the outer query, so it's re-evaluated for each outer row.
salary > ALL (S) means greater than every value in S, which is the same as greater than the maximum of S.

quiz.q: Department toppers in our data include
quiz.why: The department topper is the highest earner in each department. For HR that's Meena, who earns more than Kabir.

scenes.text: Marketing has a newsletter list and an events list. Who is on both? Who is on only one?
And the intern should see employees without salaries — a view hides the column.

steps.title: Set operations
steps.body: `q1 UNION q2` (removes duplicates), `UNION ALL` (keeps), `INTERSECT`, `EXCEPT` (MINUS in Oracle). Queries must have the same number of columns with compatible types; ORDER BY goes at the very end.

steps.title: Views
steps.body: `CREATE VIEW emp_public AS SELECT id, name, dept FROM emp;` A **view** is a stored query (virtual table): security (hide columns), simplicity, logical data independence. Simple single-table views without aggregates are usually updatable. **Materialized views** store results physically and must be refreshed.

steps.title: Data
steps.body: Tables: **dept(name, city)** — IT/Pune, HR/Delhi, Sales/Mumbai, Legal/Chennai. **emp(id, name, dept, salary, mgr)** — 1 Asha IT 90000 NULL · 2 Ravi IT 60000 1 · 3 Meena HR 50000 1 · 4 Kabir HR 45000 3 · 5 Zoya Sales 55000 1 · 6 Dev Sales 40000 5.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · EXCEPT
steps.body: `SELECT name FROM dept EXCEPT SELECT dept FROM emp;` → **Legal** (same answer as the LEFT JOIN anti-join).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · UNION vs UNION ALL
steps.body: `SELECT dept FROM emp UNION SELECT name FROM dept;` → 4 rows (HR, IT, Legal, Sales). With UNION ALL → 6 + 4 = **10 rows**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting ORDER BY inside each part of a UNION.
- Expecting a view to store data (only materialized views do).
- Using UNION when duplicates matter (counts, sums) — use UNION ALL.

activity.prompt: Use EXCEPT to list departments (from dept) that have no employees.
activity.solution: SELECT name FROM dept EXCEPT SELECT dept FROM emp;
activity.hint: The second query lists departments that do have employees.
activity.setup: CREATE TABLE dept(name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, city TEXT);INSERT INTO dept VALUES ('IT','Pune'),('HR','Delhi'),('Sales','Mumbai'),('Legal','Chennai');CREATE TABLE emp(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept TEXT REFERENCES dept(name), salary INTEGER, mgr INTEGER);INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Asha','IT',90000,NULL),(2,'Ravi','IT',60000,1),(3,'Meena','HR',50000,1),(4,'Kabir','HR',45000,3),(5,'Zoya','Sales',55000,1),(6,'Dev','Sales',40000,5);

quiz.why: UNION removes duplicates. UNION ALL keeps them.
A view is a stored query that behaves like a virtual table. It doesn't store data itself (unless materialised).
The set-difference operator EXCEPT is called MINUS in Oracle.
Views hide or reshape data, which gives logical data independence, and they restrict what users can see, which helps security.

quiz.q: UNION ALL of 6-row and 4-row results gives
quiz.why: UNION ALL doesn't remove duplicates, so 6 + 4 = 10 rows.

lessons.title: Ranking, window functions, triggers and indexes

scenes.text: 'Find the second-highest salary' — asked in countless interviews.
There are three good answers: a nested MAX, LIMIT/OFFSET, and window functions.

steps.title: Nth highest
steps.body:
- `SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp);` → 2nd highest.
- `SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;`
- `SELECT salary FROM (SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) r FROM emp) WHERE r = 2;`
Window functions: ROW_NUMBER (1,2,3,4), RANK (1,2,2,4), DENSE_RANK (1,2,2,3), SUM() OVER (PARTITION BY dept), LAG/LEAD.

steps.title: Triggers, indexes, transactions in SQL
steps.body:
- **Trigger:** code that runs automatically BEFORE/AFTER INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (e.g. write an audit row).
- **Index:** `CREATE INDEX idx_emp_dept ON emp(dept);` speeds lookups and joins; slows writes; not useful on tiny tables or low-selectivity columns.
- **Transactions:** `BEGIN; UPDATE …; UPDATE …; COMMIT;` or ROLLBACK; SAVEPOINT for partial rollback.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Rank inside departments
steps.body: `SELECT name, dept, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r FROM emp;` → HR: Meena 1, Kabir 2; IT: Asha 1, Ravi 2; Sales: Zoya 1, Dev 2. To get each department's top earner: wrap it and filter r = 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 without DISTINCT when salaries tie.
- Filtering on a window function in WHERE of the same query (not allowed — wrap in a subquery).
- Indexing every column 'just in case' (slower writes, more storage).

activity.prompt: Return the second-highest salary in emp (a single number).
activity.starter:
SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp
WHERE salary < ( /* highest */ );
activity.solution: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp);
activity.hint: The inner query returns 90000.
activity.setup: CREATE TABLE dept(name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, city TEXT);INSERT INTO dept VALUES ('IT','Pune'),('HR','Delhi'),('Sales','Mumbai'),('Legal','Chennai');CREATE TABLE emp(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept TEXT REFERENCES dept(name), salary INTEGER, mgr INTEGER);INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Asha','IT',90000,NULL),(2,'Ravi','IT',60000,1),(3,'Meena','HR',50000,1),(4,'Kabir','HR',45000,3),(5,'Zoya','Sales',55000,1),(6,'Dev','Sales',40000,5);

quiz.why: DENSE_RANK gives tied values the same rank and doesn't leave gaps: 100 → 1, 90 → 2, 90 → 2, 80 → 3.
RANK gives ties the same rank and then skips: 100 → 1, 90 → 2, 90 → 2, and the next is 4.
An index mainly speeds up reads such as lookups and joins. It slows inserts slightly.
A trigger fires automatically when a specified event (such as INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE) happens on a table.

quiz.q: To undo part of a transaction use
quiz.why: To undo part of a transaction, set a SAVEPOINT and then ROLLBACK TO it. COMMIT makes changes permanent.

questions.q: Which join returns only matching rows?
questions.why: INNER JOIN returns only the rows that match in both tables.

questions.q: UNION ALL
questions.why: UNION ALL combines results and keeps duplicate rows.

questions.q: A view stores
questions.why: A view stores a query definition, not the data, unless it's a materialised view.

questions.q: ROW_NUMBER on ties
questions.why: ROW_NUMBER assigns distinct, consecutive numbers, even to rows that tie.

questions.q: Anti-join pattern:
options: LEFT JOIN … WHERE right.key IS NULL
questions.why: The anti-join pattern uses a LEFT JOIN and keeps rows where the right key IS NULL, which are the ones with no match.

questions.q: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp e JOIN dept d ON e.dept = d.name;`
questions.why: Every employee has a department that exists in dept, so the join returns one row per employee: 6.

questions.q: Assertion (A): NOT EXISTS is safer than NOT IN for anti-joins. Reason (R): NOT IN returns no rows when the subquery contains NULL. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: NOT EXISTS is safer than NOT IN for anti-joins. R is true and explains it: NOT IN returns no rows if the subquery has a NULL, because of three-valued logic.

questions.q: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dept d LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.dept = d.name;`
questions.why: The left join starts from dept. The 6 employees each match, and Legal, with no employees, adds 1 row padded with NULLs: 7.

questions.q: Third-highest distinct salary in our emp table
questions.why: The distinct salaries in descending order are 90,000, 60,000 and 55,000. So the third-highest is 55,000.

questions.q: Case: an analyst writes `FROM dept d LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.dept = d.name WHERE e.salary > 50000` and Legal vanishes. Fix:
options: move the salary filter into the ON clause
questions.why: The WHERE filter on e.salary removes the NULL-padded row for Legal. Put the condition in the ON clause so unmatched departments are kept.

questions.q: `SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary > ALL (SELECT salary FROM emp WHERE dept='HR')` returns
questions.why: HR salaries are 50,000 and 45,000, so > ALL means more than 50,000: Asha, Ravi and Zoya.

questions.q: Correlated query: employees earning more than their manager
questions.why: Compare each employee with their manager: Ravi (60,000), Meena, Zoya report to Asha (90,000); Kabir earns less than Meena; Dev earns less than Zoya. So nobody earns more.

questions.q: `SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) = (SELECT MAX(c) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) c FROM emp GROUP BY dept));`
questions.why: The inner subquery counts employees per department, and each department has 2. The maximum is 2, so all three departments match.

questions.q: Self-join count of (employee, manager) pairs where both are in the same department
questions.why: Ravi–Asha (IT), Kabir–Meena (HR) and Dev–Zoya (Sales) share a department; Meena–Asha and Zoya–Asha do not → 3.

questions.q: Adding an index on emp(dept) helps most for
questions.why: An index helps most for selective lookups on large tables, like WHERE dept = 'HR'. On a 6-row table there's no benefit, and it slows inserts.

questions.q: Which cannot appear in a WHERE clause directly?
questions.why: Window functions can't be used directly in WHERE, since they're evaluated after it. Wrap the query in a subquery or CTE and filter outside.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Functional Dependencies & Normalization
courses.summary: Functional dependencies, Armstrong's axioms, attribute closure, candidate keys, canonical cover, 1NF/2NF/3NF/BCNF/4NF, lossless-join and dependency-preserving decomposition, and 3NF synthesis — the most-asked GATE DBMS unit.
outcomes: Learners can compute attribute closures and find all candidate keys
Learners can compute a canonical cover
Learners can identify the highest normal form of a relation
Learners can test decompositions for losslessness and dependency preservation

scenes.text: A table stores (roll, name, course, instructor, instructor_phone). The instructor's phone repeats in hundreds of rows.
Change the phone once and miss a row — an update anomaly. FDs explain why.

steps.title: Anomalies and FDs
steps.body:
Bad designs suffer **insertion, deletion and update anomalies** due to redundancy.
An FD **X → Y** holds if any two tuples that agree on X also agree on Y. Trivial if Y ⊆ X.
**Armstrong's axioms** (sound and complete): reflexivity (Y ⊆ X ⇒ X → Y), augmentation (X → Y ⇒ XZ → YZ), transitivity. Derived: union, decomposition, pseudo-transitivity (X → Y, WY → Z ⇒ WX → Z).

steps.title: Attribute closure X⁺
steps.body: Start with X; repeatedly add the RHS of any FD whose LHS ⊆ current set; stop when nothing changes. Uses: test X → Y (is Y ⊆ X⁺?), test superkey (X⁺ = all attributes).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Closure
steps.body:
R(A, B, C, D, E), F = {A → B, B → C, CD → E}.
- A⁺: A → B → C → **{A, B, C}** (CD → E needs D).
- AD⁺: A, D → B → C → CD → E → **{A, B, C, D, E}** ⇒ AD is a superkey.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Implied FD?
steps.body: Does F imply AD → E? AD⁺ contains E → **yes**. Does F imply B → A? B⁺ = {B, C} → **no**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Stopping the closure after one pass — loop until no change.
- Splitting the LHS: from AB → C you cannot infer A → C.
- Confusing an FD holding in a sample instance with holding on the schema.

activity.prompt: Attribute closure. Line 1: the starting attributes (letters, e.g. AD). Line 2: FDs like A->B,B->C,CD->E. Print the closure letters sorted.
activity.starter:
x = set(input().strip())
fds = []
for f in input().split(','):
    l, r = f.split('->')
    fds.append((set(l), set(r)))
# repeat until no FD adds anything
activity.hint: Use set operations: l <= x tests subset.

quiz.why: A dependency X → Y is trivial when Y is a subset of X, because it holds automatically.

quiz.q: Which is NOT an Armstrong axiom?
quiz.why: Armstrong's axioms are reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity. Commutativity isn't one of them.

quiz.q: From AB → C we can conclude
quiz.why: From AB → C, augmentation gives ABD → C, since adding attributes to the left side keeps the dependency true. A → C or B → C needn't hold.

quiz.q: With F = {A → B, B → C}, A⁺ =
quiz.why: A determines B, and B determines C, so A⁺ = {A, B, C}.

quiz.q: X is a superkey of R iff
quiz.why: X is a superkey exactly when its closure contains every attribute of R, X⁺ = R.

scenes.text: GATE asks 'how many candidate keys?' almost every year.
A quick trick: attributes that never appear on any right side must be in every key.

steps.title: Finding all candidate keys
steps.body:
1. Attributes not on any RHS (call them *core*) must be in every key.
2. If core⁺ = R, core is the only key.
3. Otherwise add other attributes (prefer those that appear on LHS) one at a time, then two at a time…, keeping only **minimal** sets whose closure is R.
Prime attribute = belongs to some candidate key.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Several keys
steps.body:
R(A, B, C, D, E), F = {AB → C, C → D, D → B, D → E}.
- A never on RHS → in every key. A⁺ = {A}.
- AB⁺ = ABCDE ✓, AC⁺ = A C D B E ✓, AD⁺ = A D B E C ✓, AE⁺ = AE ✗.
- Candidate keys: **AB, AC, AD**. Prime: A, B, C, D; non-prime: E.

steps.title: Canonical (minimal) cover
steps.body: Steps: (1) split RHS into single attributes; (2) remove **extraneous LHS attributes** (in XA → B, A is extraneous if X⁺ under F contains B); (3) remove **redundant FDs** (an FD is redundant if implied by the others); (4) merge FDs with the same LHS.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Canonical cover
steps.body:
F = {A → BC, B → C, A → B, AB → C}.
- Split: A → B, A → C, B → C, A → B (dup), AB → C.
- AB → C: B is extraneous? A⁺ = {A, B, C} contains C → reduce to A → C (duplicate).
- A → C redundant (A → B, B → C).
- Canonical cover: **{A → B, B → C}**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reporting a superkey (e.g. ABC) as a candidate key — check minimality.
- Removing an FD and its extraneous attributes in the wrong order — remove extraneous LHS attributes first.
- Forgetting that a relation can have exponentially many keys.

activity.prompt: R(A, B, C, D) with F = {A → B, B → C, C → A}. How many candidate keys?

quiz.q: An attribute never on any RHS must be
quiz.why: If an attribute never appears on the right of any FD, nothing determines it, so it must be in every candidate key.
A prime attribute is one that belongs to at least one candidate key.

quiz.q: Canonical cover of {A → B, B → C, A → C}
quiz.why: A → C follows from A → B and B → C, so it's redundant. The canonical cover is {A → B, B → C}.

quiz.q: In XA → B, A is extraneous if
quiz.why: In XA → B, attribute A is extraneous if B can already be derived from X alone, that is if X⁺ contains B.

quiz.q: R(A,B,C) with F = {A → B, B → C}: candidate key
quiz.why: A⁺ = {A, B, C}, since A → B and B → C. So A alone is a key and is minimal.

scenes.text: Each normal form forbids one more kind of redundancy.
Most real designs aim for 3NF or BCNF.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **1NF:** all attribute values atomic (no repeating groups or multivalued cells).
- **2NF:** 1NF + no **partial dependency** (non-prime attribute depending on a proper subset of a candidate key). Only an issue with composite keys.
- **3NF:** for every non-trivial X → A: X is a superkey **or** A is prime. (Equivalently no transitive dependency of a non-prime on a key.)
- **BCNF:** for every non-trivial X → A: X is a superkey.
BCNF ⊂ 3NF ⊂ 2NF ⊂ 1NF. A relation with only two attributes is always in BCNF.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Find the highest NF
steps.body:
R(A, B, C, D), F = {AB → C, C → D}. Key: AB (A, B never on RHS; AB⁺ = ABCD).
- 2NF? Partial dependency means A → something or B → something non-prime; A⁺ = A, B⁺ = B → none → **2NF ✓**.
- 3NF? C → D: C not a superkey, D non-prime → ✗.
- Highest: **2NF**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · 3NF but not BCNF
steps.body:
R(A, B, C), F = {AB → C, C → B}. Keys: AB and AC. Prime: A, B, C (all).
- C → B: C not a superkey but B is prime → 3NF ✓.
- BCNF requires C to be a superkey → ✗.
- Highest: **3NF**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 · Partial dependency
steps.body: R(roll, course, name, grade), key (roll, course), roll → name. name is non-prime and depends on part of the key → **not 2NF** (highest 1NF). Fix: Student(roll, name), Result(roll, course, grade).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Checking 2NF on a relation with single-attribute keys (it is automatically 2NF).
- Forgetting the 'A is prime' escape clause in 3NF.
- Believing BCNF decomposition always preserves dependencies.

activity.prompt: Highest normal form?

items.text: R(A,B,C), A → B, A → C (key A)

quiz.why: Second normal form removes partial dependencies, where a non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite key.
In a relation with only two attributes, any non-trivial FD has a key as its left side, so it's always in BCNF.

quiz.q: 3NF allows X → A with X not superkey if
quiz.why: 3NF allows X → A even when X isn't a superkey, provided A is a prime attribute. BCNF doesn't allow that exception.

quiz.q: R(A,B,C), F = {A → B, B → C}, key A: highest NF
quiz.why: The key is A, and B → C makes C transitively dependent on A through B (B is not a key, C is non-prime). So 3NF fails but 2NF holds, since A is a single-attribute key.
Repeating groups mean non-atomic values, which break first normal form.

scenes.text: Splitting a table reduces redundancy — but a bad split creates fake rows when you join back.
Two tests keep splits safe: lossless join and dependency preservation.

steps.title: Tests
steps.body:
- **Lossless join (binary):** R → R1, R2 is lossless iff (R1 ∩ R2) → R1 or (R1 ∩ R2) → R2 is in F⁺ (common attributes form a superkey of one side).
- **Dependency preserving:** (F₁ ∪ F₂ ∪ …)⁺ = F⁺, where Fᵢ are the FDs of F⁺ that involve only Rᵢ's attributes.
- **3NF synthesis** (always lossless and dependency preserving): one relation per FD of the canonical cover; add a relation containing a candidate key if none has one; drop subsumed relations.
- **BCNF decomposition:** pick a violating X → Y, split into (X ∪ Y) and (R − Y + X), repeat. Always lossless, **not always** dependency preserving.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Lossless?
steps.body:
R(A, B, C), F = {A → B}. Split R1(A, B), R2(A, C): common A, A → AB = R1 → **lossless**.
R(A, B, C, D), F = {A → B, C → D} split into (A, B), (C, D): common ∅ → **lossy** (join gives a Cartesian product).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · 3NF synthesis
steps.body:
R(A, B, C, D), F = {A → B, C → D}. Key AC.
- From FDs: R1(A, B), R2(C, D). No relation contains AC → add R3(A, C).
- Result **{(A, B), (C, D), (A, C)}** — lossless and dependency preserving, all BCNF here.

steps.title: Solved example 3 · BCNF can lose an FD
steps.body: R(A, B, C), F = {AB → C, C → B}. BCNF violation C → B → split into (C, B) and (A, C). Lossless (common C → B). But AB → C cannot be checked inside either table → **not dependency preserving**. 3NF keeps R as is.

steps.title: Beyond BCNF
steps.body: **Multivalued dependency** X ↠ Y: the set of Y-values for an X is independent of the other attributes (e.g. a teacher's courses and languages). **4NF:** every non-trivial MVD X ↠ Y has X a superkey. **5NF/PJNF** deals with join dependencies.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Testing losslessness with the union instead of the intersection.
- Thinking 3NF synthesis may be lossy — adding a key relation guarantees losslessness.
- Claiming every relation has a BCNF decomposition that preserves dependencies.

statements.why: Each split uses a superkey of one part.

statements.s: 3NF synthesis is lossless and dependency preserving.
statements.why: That is why 3NF is the practical target.

statements.s: Splitting R(A,B,C,D) into (A,B) and (C,D) with no FD across is lossless.

quiz.q: Binary decomposition is lossless iff the common attributes
options: functionally determine one of the parts
quiz.why: A binary decomposition R1, R2 is lossless iff the common attributes functionally determine R1 or R2 (are a superkey of one of them).

quiz.q: 3NF synthesis adds a key relation to ensure
quiz.why: 3NF synthesis adds a relation containing a candidate key, so the decomposition is lossless as well as dependency-preserving.

quiz.q: Which is guaranteed in BCNF decomposition?
quiz.why: BCNF decomposition always gives a lossless join, but dependency preservation can't always be guaranteed.

quiz.q: Teacher ↠ Course in (Teacher, Course, Language) violates
quiz.why: A non-trivial multivalued dependency whose left side isn't a superkey violates 4NF.
The common attribute B determines C, so it's a key of (B, C). So the decomposition into (A, B) and (B, C) is lossless.

questions.q: Update anomalies are caused by
questions.why: Update anomalies arise from redundancy: the same fact is stored in many rows, so changing one copy leaves the others inconsistent.

questions.q: Attribute closure is used to
questions.why: Attribute closure is used to test whether a set of attributes is a superkey and to check whether an FD is implied.

questions.q: BCNF requires every determinant to be a
questions.why: BCNF requires that for every non-trivial FD X → Y, X is a superkey.

questions.q: R(A,B,C,D), F = {A → B, B → C, C → D}: A⁺
questions.why: Following the chain A → B → C → D gives A⁺ = {A, B, C, D}.

questions.q: Which NF eliminates partial dependencies?
questions.why: Second normal form (2NF) eliminates partial dependencies.

questions.q: Armstrong's axioms are
questions.why: Armstrong's axioms are sound (they derive only valid FDs) and complete (they derive all implied FDs).

questions.q: Assertion (A): Every BCNF relation is in 3NF. Reason (R): BCNF's condition is a stricter version of 3NF's. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: every BCNF relation is in 3NF. R is true and explains it: BCNF's condition (every determinant is a superkey) is a stricter version of 3NF, with no exception for prime attributes.

questions.q: R(A,B,C,D,E), F = {A → B, BC → D, D → E}. Candidate key:
questions.why: A and C never appear on the right side of an FD, so they must be in the key. AC⁺: A → B, BC → D, D → E gives {A, B, C, D, E}. So AC is the candidate key.

questions.q: R(A,B,C,D), F = {AB → CD, D → A}. Candidate keys:
questions.why: B never appears on a right side, so it's in every key. AB⁺ = ABCD. BD⁺ = B D → A (via D → A) → C, D (via AB → CD) = ABCD. So AB and BD are keys.

questions.q: Case: Orders(order_id, product_id, qty, product_name) with key (order_id, product_id) and product_id → product_name. Highest NF and fix:
questions.why: product_id → product_name depends on only part of the key (order_id, product_id), a partial dependency, so the table is in 1NF only. Move product_name into Product(product_id, product_name).

questions.q: R(A,B,C,D,E,F) with F = {A → BC, D → E, AD → F}. Number of candidate keys
questions.why: A and D never appear on the right side, so they must be in every key. AD⁺ includes B, C (from A), E (from D) and F, so AD is the only candidate key.

questions.q: R(A,B,C,D) with F = {A → B, B → A, C → D}. Candidate keys:
questions.why: C never appears on the right of an FD whose left... in fact C isn't determined by anything else, so it must be in every key, and A ↔ B are equivalent. AC⁺ = ABCD and BC⁺ = ABCD, so the keys are AC and BC.

questions.q: Canonical cover of {A → B, AB → C, C → A, A → C}
questions.why: AB → C: B is extraneous because A⁺ already contains C (via A → C), so it becomes the duplicate A → C. Nothing else is redundant: {A → B, A → C, C → A} (equivalently A → BC, C → A).

questions.q: R(A,B,C,D), F = {A → B, C → D}; decomposition {(A,B), (C,D), (A,C)} is
questions.why: The decomposition is dependency preserving, since A → B and C → D sit in (A, B) and (C, D). It's lossless because (A, C) contains the key AC. This is the 3NF synthesis result.

questions.q: R(A,B,C), F = {A → B, B → C, C → A}. Highest NF
questions.why: A → B → C → A means each of A, B and C determines the others, so each is a key. Every FD's left side is a key, so the relation is in BCNF.

questions.q: Number of superkeys of R(A,B,C,D) with F = {A → B, B → C, C → D, D → A}
questions.why: Every single attribute is a key → every non-empty subset is a superkey: 2⁴ − 1 = 15.
