courses.title: Unit 6 · Transactions & Concurrency Control
courses.summary: ACID properties and transaction states, schedules, conflict and view serializability with precedence graphs, recoverable and cascadeless schedules, two-phase locking variants, timestamp ordering, and deadlock handling (wait–die, wound–wait).
outcomes: Learners can test conflict serializability with a precedence graph
Learners can classify schedules as recoverable, cascadeless or strict
Learners can apply basic, strict and rigorous 2PL
Learners can apply timestamp-ordering rules and Thomas' write rule

scenes.text: Neha sends ₹500 via UPI. Her bank debits her; the receiving bank must credit her friend.
If power fails between the two steps, the money must not vanish.

steps.title: ACID
steps.body:
- **Atomicity:** all or nothing (recovery manager, undo log).
- **Consistency:** a correct transaction moves the database from one consistent state to another (application + constraints).
- **Isolation:** concurrent execution looks like some serial order (concurrency-control manager).
- **Durability:** once committed, changes survive failures (redo log, stable storage).

steps.title: States
steps.body: Active → Partially committed (last statement executed) → Committed; or Active/Partially committed → Failed → Aborted (rolled back; then restart or kill). Committed and Aborted are terminal.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Which property?
steps.body:
(a) Crash after debit but before credit; on restart the debit is undone → **atomicity**.
(b) A committed booking survives a server reboot → **durability**.
(c) Two clerks booking the last seat never both succeed → **isolation**.
(d) Total money in the bank is unchanged by a transfer → **consistency**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Counting schedules
steps.body: T1 has 2 operations, T2 has 3. Serial schedules: 2! = **2**. All interleavings preserving each transaction's internal order: (2 + 3)! / (2! · 3!) = **10**. For n transactions, n! serial schedules.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assigning consistency to the DBMS alone — the programmer's logic must be correct too.
- Thinking 'partially committed' means durable — it is not yet committed.
- Counting all permutations of operations instead of order-preserving interleavings.

activity.prompt: Match the property to the DBMS component that guarantees it

quiz.why: Atomicity means a transaction is all-or-nothing: either all its changes happen or none.

quiz.q: After the last statement executes, a transaction is
quiz.why: After its last statement runs, a transaction is partially committed. It becomes committed only once the changes are safely recorded.

quiz.q: Interleavings of T1 (3 ops) and T2 (3 ops)
quiz.why: Interleavings keep each transaction's own order. With 6 operations, choose which 3 positions belong to T1: 6!/(3!·3!) = 720/36 = 20.
A serial schedule runs the transactions one after another, so each ordering of 4 transactions is a serial schedule: 4! = 24.

quiz.q: Committed data surviving a crash is
quiz.why: Durability means that once a transaction commits, its changes survive crashes and power failures.

scenes.text: Two transactions interleave reads and writes on A and B.
Draw an arrow for every conflict. If the arrows form a cycle, no serial order matches.

steps.title: Conflicts and precedence graphs
steps.body:
Two operations **conflict** if they are from different transactions, on the same item, and at least one is a write (RW, WR, WW).
A schedule is **conflict serializable** if it can be turned into a serial schedule by swapping adjacent non-conflicting operations ⇔ its **precedence graph** (edge Ti → Tj if an operation of Ti conflicts with and precedes one of Tj) is **acyclic**. A topological order gives an equivalent serial schedule.

steps.title: View serializability
steps.body: View equivalent to a serial schedule if: same initial reads, same reads-from relationships, same final writes. Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable; the converse fails only with **blind writes** (write without a prior read). Testing view serializability is NP-complete.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Cycle
steps.body:
S: R1(A) W2(A) R2(B) W1(B).
- R1(A) before W2(A) → T1 → T2.
- R2(B) before W1(B) → T2 → T1.
- Cycle → **not conflict serializable**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · View but not conflict
steps.body:
S: R1(A) W2(A) W1(A) W3(A).
- Edges: T1 → T2 (R1–W2), T2 → T1 (W2–W1), T1 → T3, T2 → T3 → cycle → not conflict serializable.
- View: T1 reads initial A, final write by T3; serial T1 T2 T3 has the same → **view serializable** (thanks to blind writes W2, W3).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding edges for two reads (RR never conflicts).
- Adding edges between operations of the same transaction.
- Thinking a cycle-free graph has only one equivalent serial order.

activity.prompt: Conflict-serializability test. Input: one line of operations like R1(A) W2(A) R2(B) W1(B) (single-digit transaction ids, one-letter items). Print SERIALIZABLE or NOT SERIALIZABLE.
activity.starter:
ops = input().split()
p = [(o[0], o[1], o[3]) for o in ops]  # (R/W, txn, item)
edges = {}
# add edge ti->tj for each conflicting pair (i before j), then look for a cycle
activity.hint: Depth-first search with a recursion stack finds cycles.

quiz.why: Two operations conflict if they belong to different transactions, touch the same item, and at least one is a write. R1(A) and W2(A) fit.
A schedule is conflict serializable exactly when its precedence graph has no cycle (is acyclic).

quiz.q: View-serializable but not conflict-serializable schedules contain
quiz.why: Schedules that are view serializable but not conflict serializable contain blind writes (writes without a prior read of the item).
Testing view serializability is NP-complete in general, unlike conflict serializability, which needs only a cycle check.

quiz.q: S: R1(A) R2(A) W1(B) W2(B). Edges:
quiz.why: Only W1(B) before W2(B) is a conflict across the transactions. The reads of A don't conflict with each other. So the only edge is T1 → T2.

scenes.text: T2 reads a balance T1 wrote, and commits. Then T1 aborts.
T2 acted on money that never existed — the schedule is not recoverable.

steps.title: Recoverable, cascadeless, strict
steps.body:
- **Recoverable:** if Tj reads an item written by Ti, Ti commits **before** Tj commits.
- **Cascadeless (ACA):** transactions read only committed data (no dirty reads) → no cascading rollbacks.
- **Strict:** no read or write of an item until the last transaction that wrote it commits/aborts.
Strict ⊂ Cascadeless ⊂ Recoverable.

steps.title: Lock-based protocols
steps.body:
Shared (S) locks for read, exclusive (X) for write; S–S compatible, others not.
- **Two-phase locking (2PL):** growing phase (acquire, no release) then shrinking phase (release, no acquire). Guarantees **conflict serializability** (lock point order); does **not** prevent deadlocks or cascading rollbacks.
- **Strict 2PL:** hold all X locks until commit → strict schedules.
- **Rigorous 2PL:** hold all locks until commit → serial order = commit order.
- **Conservative 2PL:** lock everything up front → deadlock-free.
Lock conversion: upgrade S → X (growing), downgrade X → S (shrinking).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Classify
steps.body:
S: W1(A) R2(A) C2 C1 → T2 read T1's dirty write and committed first → **not recoverable**.
S: W1(A) R2(A) C1 C2 → recoverable but not cascadeless (dirty read).
S: W1(A) C1 R2(A) C2 → **cascadeless (and strict)**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Is it 2PL?
steps.body: T1: X(A) R(A) W(A) U(A) X(B) R(B) W(B) U(B). It releases A before acquiring B → **violates 2PL**. Fix: X(A) … X(B) … U(A) U(B).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming 2PL prevents deadlock (only conservative 2PL does).
- Confusing recoverable (commit order) with cascadeless (no dirty reads).
- Releasing a lock and later acquiring another in 'basic 2PL'.

activity.prompt: Classify each schedule (C = commit)

quiz.why: Two-phase locking (acquire all locks, then release) guarantees conflict serializability, with transactions ordered by their lock points. It doesn't prevent deadlocks.

quiz.q: Strict 2PL holds which locks until commit?
quiz.why: Strict 2PL keeps all exclusive (X) locks until commit or abort, so no one can read uncommitted writes and cascading rollbacks are avoided.
Conservative 2PL has a transaction lock everything it needs before starting. Since it never waits while holding locks, deadlocks can't occur.
A dirty read is reading data written by a transaction that hasn't committed yet, which may be rolled back.
The hierarchy is strict ⊂ cascadeless ⊂ recoverable, so every cascadeless schedule is recoverable.

lessons.title: Timestamps, deadlock schemes and isolation levels

story.title: First come, first served — by ticket

scenes.text: Each transaction gets a ticket number (timestamp) when it starts.
Conflicts are resolved so the outcome equals running them in ticket order.

steps.title: Basic timestamp ordering (TO)
steps.body:
Each item Q has W-TS(Q), R-TS(Q).
- Ti reads Q: if TS(Ti) < W-TS(Q) → **abort Ti** (it would read a 'future' value); else read, R-TS = max(R-TS, TS(Ti)).
- Ti writes Q: if TS(Ti) < R-TS(Q) → abort; if TS(Ti) < W-TS(Q) → abort (basic) or **ignore the write (Thomas' write rule)**; else write, W-TS = TS(Ti).
TO is deadlock-free (no waiting) but may starve and cause cascading aborts unless made strict. Thomas' rule allows some view-serializable schedules.

steps.title: Deadlock prevention with timestamps
steps.body:
Older transaction = smaller timestamp.
- **Wait–die (non-preemptive):** older requesting a lock held by younger **waits**; younger requesting from older **dies** (aborts, restarts with the same timestamp).
- **Wound–wait (preemptive):** older **wounds** (aborts) the younger holder; younger requesting from older **waits**.
Both avoid starvation because restarted transactions keep their original timestamps.

steps.title: SQL isolation levels
steps.body: READ UNCOMMITTED (dirty reads possible), READ COMMITTED (no dirty reads), REPEATABLE READ (no non-repeatable reads; phantoms possible per the standard), SERIALIZABLE (no phantoms). Many systems implement snapshot isolation / MVCC.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · TO rule
steps.body: TS(T1) = 5, TS(T2) = 10. Item Q: R-TS = 10 (T2 read it). T1 now tries to write Q: TS(T1) = 5 < R-TS = 10 → **T1 aborts** (T2 already read the old value).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Wait–die vs wound–wait
steps.body:
T5 (older) wants a lock held by T9 (younger): wait–die → T5 **waits**; wound–wait → T9 **is aborted**.
T9 wants a lock held by T5: wait–die → T9 **dies**; wound–wait → T9 **waits**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping the rules of wait–die and wound–wait (remember: in both, the *younger* is the one that gets aborted).
- Thinking Thomas' rule ignores reads — it ignores only obsolete writes.
- Giving a restarted transaction a new timestamp (causes starvation).

a.text: Wound–wait is in use. T3 (older, TS 3) requests an X lock on item A, held by T7 (younger, TS 7). What happens?

choices.label: T3 waits for T7
choices.feedback: That would be wait–die's rule for an older requester.

choices.label: T7 is wounded (rolled back) and T3 gets the lock

w1.text: Not in wound–wait. Remember: older transactions never wait for younger ones in wound–wait. Try the next case.

b.text: Now T7 restarts and requests a lock held by T3. Under wound–wait, what happens?

end.text: Summary: wound–wait — older wounds, younger waits. Wait–die — older waits, younger dies. Restarted transactions keep their original timestamp, so they eventually become the oldest and finish.

quiz.q: In basic TO, a read by Ti with TS(Ti) < W-TS(Q)
quiz.why: In basic timestamp ordering, if Ti is older than the last writer of Q (TS(Ti) < W-TS(Q)), it would read a value from the future, so Ti is aborted.
Thomas' write rule ignores an obsolete write, which is a write that an already-newer write would overwrite, instead of aborting.

quiz.q: Under wait–die, a younger requester of a lock held by an older one
quiz.why: In wait–die, an older transaction may wait for a younger one, but a younger one requesting a lock held by an older transaction dies (is aborted).
Timestamp ordering never makes a transaction wait, so no deadlock can form. It can abort transactions instead.

quiz.q: Which isolation level prevents dirty reads but allows non-repeatable reads?
quiz.why: READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads, but a row read twice may change in between (non-repeatable read). REPEATABLE READ prevents that.

questions.q: ACID's 'I' stands for
questions.why: The I in ACID is isolation: concurrent transactions don't interfere with each other.

questions.q: RR operations on the same item
questions.why: Two reads of the same item don't conflict, since the order in which they occur doesn't change the result.

questions.q: 2PL's two phases are
questions.why: Two-phase locking has a growing phase, where locks are acquired, and a shrinking phase, where they're released. No lock is acquired after the first release.

questions.q: A schedule with a cyclic precedence graph is
questions.why: A cycle in the precedence graph means the schedule isn't conflict serializable, because no serial order can respect all the dependencies.

questions.q: Interleavings of T1 (2 ops) and T2 (2 ops)
questions.why: Choose which 2 of the 4 positions belong to T1: C(4,2) = 4!/(2!2!) = 6.

questions.q: Dirty reads are prevented in
questions.why: Cascadeless (avoid cascading aborts) schedules allow reads only of committed data, which prevents dirty reads.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable. Reason (R): Conflict equivalence implies view equivalence. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable. R is true and explains it: conflict equivalence is the stronger notion and implies view equivalence.

questions.q: S: R1(A) R2(A) W1(A) W2(A). Precedence edges
questions.why: R2(A) before W1(A) gives T2 → T1. R1(A) before W2(A), and W1(A) before W2(A), give T1 → T2. So there are edges both ways, a cycle.

questions.q: Basic 2PL can suffer from
questions.why: Basic 2PL can deadlock (two transactions wait for each other's locks) and can have cascading rollbacks, because locks can be released before commit.

questions.q: Case: a ticketing system sees two users both 'buy' the last seat. Which ACID property failed?
questions.why: Two users interfering and both buying the last seat is a concurrency problem. Isolation failed, as they should have been serialised.

questions.q: S: R2(B) W2(B) R1(A) R3(B) W1(A) W3(B). Equivalent serial order
questions.why: The only conflict across transactions is on B: T2's operations come before T3's, so the edge is T2 → T3. T1 touches only A, so it is independent. Any order with T2 before T3 works.

questions.q: TS(T1) = 10. W-TS(Q) = 15, R-TS(Q) = 5. T1 writes Q under Thomas' rule:
questions.why: TS(T1) = 10 is less than W-TS(Q) = 15, but not less than R-TS(Q) = 5. Nobody newer has read Q, so the write is just obsolete, and Thomas' rule ignores it.

questions.q: Wound–wait: T2 (TS 2) requests lock held by T6 (TS 6)
questions.why: In wound–wait, an older transaction requesting a lock held by a younger one wounds it. T2 (TS 2) is older than T6, so T6 is aborted.

questions.q: Schedule W1(A) R2(A) W2(B) C2 A1 (T1 aborts) is
questions.why: T2 read T1's uncommitted write and committed before T1. When T1 aborts, T2's committed result depends on data that vanishes, so it isn't recoverable.

questions.q: Which statement is FALSE?
questions.why: The false statement is that basic 2PL avoids deadlocks. Basic 2PL can deadlock. Conservative 2PL avoids them.

questions.q: Number of conflict-equivalent serial schedules for an acyclic precedence graph with T1 → T2, T1 → T3 and no other edges
questions.why: T1 must come first. T2 and T3 have no edge between them, so they can go in either order: T1, T2, T3 or T1, T3, T2. That's 2.

courses.summary: File organisation and block access costs, primary/clustering/secondary and dense/sparse indexes, B-trees and B+ trees with order calculations, static and dynamic hashing, query-processing basics, and log-based recovery with WAL and checkpoints.

Learners can compute the order of B+ tree nodes and tree height
Learners can compare B-trees, B+ trees and hashing
Learners can perform undo/redo recovery from a log

story.title: Finding a book in a library

scenes.text: A library with 1 lakh books: scanning every shelf is slow; a catalogue card points straight to the shelf.
Indexes are a database's catalogue.

steps.title: Basics
steps.body:
- **Blocking factor** bfr = ⌊block size / record size⌋ records per block (unspanned). Blocks b = ⌈r / bfr⌉.
- **Heap file:** linear search ≈ b/2 block reads on average (b worst). **Sorted file:** binary search ⌈log₂ b⌉.
- **Primary index:** on the ordering key of a sorted file; **sparse** (one entry per block).
- **Clustering index:** on a non-key ordering field.
- **Secondary index:** on a non-ordering field; **dense** (one entry per record).
- **Multilevel index:** index on the index; fan-out fo = ⌊block / entry⌋; levels ≈ ⌈log_fo(entries)⌉.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Binary search vs primary index
steps.body:
r = 30,000 records, record 100 B, block 1024 B → bfr = 10 → b = 3000 blocks.
- Binary search: ⌈log₂ 3000⌉ = **12** block reads.
- Primary index: entry = key 9 B + pointer 6 B = 15 B → 68 entries/block; 3000 entries → ⌈3000/68⌉ = 45 index blocks → ⌈log₂ 45⌉ = 6, + 1 data block = **7** reads.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Multilevel index
steps.body: Same index with fan-out 68: level 1 has 45 blocks; level 2 needs ⌈45/68⌉ = 1 block. Levels = 2 → access = 2 + 1 = **3** block reads.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Rounding bfr up (it must be floored for unspanned records).
- Forgetting the final data-block access.
- Saying a secondary index can be sparse — it must be dense (file not ordered on that field).

activity.prompt: 1,00,000 records of 200 B in 4096 B blocks (unspanned). How many blocks does the file need?

quiz.q: Sparse index has one entry per
quiz.why: A sparse index has one entry per block (not per record), and it requires the file to be sorted on the indexed key.
A secondary index is on a field that the file isn't sorted by, so it must have an entry for every record: it's dense.

quiz.q: Binary search on 1024 blocks needs about
quiz.why: Binary search halves the range each time, so 1024 = 2¹⁰ blocks need about 10 block reads.

quiz.q: bfr for 512 B blocks and 100 B records
quiz.why: The blocking factor is ⌊512/100⌋ = 5 records per block. We take the floor since a record can't be split across blocks here.

quiz.q: A file can have how many primary (ordering-key) indexes?
quiz.why: A file can be physically ordered in only one way, so it has at most one primary (ordering-key) index.

scenes.text: Every insert and delete keeps all leaves at the same depth.
That's why almost every relational database uses B+ trees for indexes.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body:
**B-tree of order p:** each node has ≤ p children and ≤ p − 1 keys; non-root internal nodes ≥ ⌈p/2⌉ children; keys and data pointers in all nodes.
**B+ tree:** internal nodes hold only keys + child pointers (higher fan-out); **all record pointers are in the leaves**, which are linked for range scans. Every search goes to a leaf (height + 1 node reads). Insertion splits overflowing nodes and pushes a key up; deletion merges/redistributes.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Order of nodes
steps.body:
Block 512 B, key 10 B, block pointer 6 B, record pointer 7 B.
- **Internal** (p pointers, p − 1 keys): 6p + 10(p − 1) ≤ 512 → 16p ≤ 522 → **p = 32**.
- **Leaf** (q key–record-pointer pairs + 1 next pointer): 17q + 6 ≤ 512 → **q = 29**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Height for 1 million keys
steps.body: Internal fan-out 32 (assume ~full), leaves hold 29 keys. Leaves needed ≈ ⌈10⁶ / 29⌉ = 34,483. Internal levels: 32 → 32² = 1024 → 32³ = 32,768 (< 34,483) → 32⁴ — so **4 internal levels + leaf level**: about 5 node reads, + 1 for the record = 6. Real trees are ~69% full, giving one more level at most.

steps.title: Solved example 3 · Insert with split
steps.body: B+ tree, leaf capacity 3 keys. Leaf [10, 20, 30] receives 25 → [10, 20, 25, 30] overflows → split into [10, 20] and [25, 30]; copy **25** up into the parent (in a B+ tree the separator stays in the leaf; in a B-tree the middle key moves up).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the record-pointer size for internal nodes of a B+ tree (they have block pointers only).
- Forgetting the p − 1 keys term.
- Thinking B+ tree internal keys must also exist as records — they are separators.

activity.prompt: Block 1024 B, key 12 B, block pointer 8 B. Order p of a B+ tree internal node (p·8 + (p−1)·12 ≤ 1024)?

quiz.q: Range queries are efficient in B+ trees because
quiz.why: B+ tree leaves are linked in key order, so a range query finds the start and then scans the leaves sequentially.

quiz.q: Record pointers in a B+ tree are stored in
quiz.why: In a B+ tree, the record (data) pointers are stored only in the leaf nodes. Internal nodes only guide the search.

quiz.q: Minimum children of a non-root internal node of order p
quiz.why: A non-root internal node must be at least half full, so it has at least ⌈p/2⌉ children.

quiz.q: Why is B+ tree fan-out higher than B-tree's?
options: no data pointers in internal nodes
quiz.why: B+ internal nodes have no data pointers, so more keys and child pointers fit in a block. That gives a higher fan-out and a shorter tree.

quiz.q: In a B+ tree split, the separator key is
quiz.why: When a B+ tree leaf splits, the separator key is copied up to the parent and also stays in the leaf. In an internal node split, the key moves up.

scenes.text: A gym assigns lockers by member ID mod 100. Finding a locker takes one step — unless two members collide.
Hashing gives O(1) equality lookups but cannot do ranges.

steps.title: Hashing
steps.body:
- **Static hashing:** h(K) mod M buckets; overflow chains when buckets fill; poor when the file grows.
- **Extendible hashing:** directory of 2^d pointers (global depth d); buckets have local depth; a full bucket splits, and the directory doubles only when local depth = global depth.
- **Linear hashing:** buckets split in a fixed round-robin order, no directory.
Hash indexes support equality, not range queries.

steps.title: Query processing
steps.body:
Parse → translate to relational algebra → optimise (equivalence rules: push σ down, push π down, reorder joins) → choose access paths and join algorithms → execute.
Join algorithms: **nested loop** (block nested loop cost ≈ b_R + b_R × b_S with one buffer block per relation), **index nested loop**, **sort–merge**, **hash join**. Use the smaller relation as the outer relation.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Extendible hashing
steps.body: Global depth 2 (directory 00, 01, 10, 11), bucket capacity 2. Bucket for 01 has local depth 2 and is full; inserting another key with suffix 01 → local depth = global depth → **directory doubles** to depth 3 (8 entries) and the bucket splits into 001 and 101.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Nested-loop cost
steps.body: b_R = 100 blocks, b_S = 400 blocks, one block buffer each. R outer: 100 + 100 × 400 = **40,100** block transfers. S outer: 400 + 400 × 100 = 40,400. With enough memory to hold R entirely: 100 + 400 = **500**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing hashing for range queries.
- Doubling the extendible-hashing directory on every split.
- Putting the larger relation as the outer loop.

activity.prompt: Block nested-loop join: b_R = 50 blocks (outer), b_S = 200 blocks, one buffer block each. Block transfers = b_R + b_R × b_S?

quiz.why: A hash index scatters keys, so it keeps no order. It's good for equality lookups, but poor for range searches.

quiz.q: Extendible hashing doubles the directory when
options: a full bucket's local depth equals global depth
quiz.why: In extendible hashing, if a full bucket's local depth equals the global depth, the directory must double before the bucket can split. Otherwise just the bucket splits.

quiz.q: Pushing selections down the query tree
quiz.why: Pushing selections down the query tree filters rows early, so intermediate results are smaller and later operations are cheaper.

quiz.q: Best outer relation for block nested-loop
quiz.why: Using the smaller relation as the outer one in block nested-loop join gives fewer outer iterations, so the inner relation is scanned fewer times.
Linear hashing grows by splitting buckets one at a time in round-robin order, with no directory.

scenes.text: Before changing any balance, the bank writes the old and new values in a diary.
After a crash, it reads the diary: redo what was committed, undo what was not.

steps.title: Logs and rules
steps.body:
Log records: <T start>, <T, X, old, new>, <T commit>, <T abort>.
- **Write-ahead logging (WAL):** the log record must reach stable storage *before* the data page is written; all log records of T are flushed before T commits.
- **Deferred modification:** writes applied only after commit → only **redo** needed.
- **Immediate modification:** writes may reach disk before commit → **undo** (uncommitted, in reverse order) and **redo** (committed, in forward order).
- **Checkpoint:** flush log and dirty pages, write <checkpoint L> (L = active transactions); recovery starts scanning from the last checkpoint.
- **ARIES** (used by many systems): analysis, redo (repeat history), undo phases with LSNs and compensation log records.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Recover after crash
steps.body:
Log: <T1 start> <T1, A, 100, 50> <T2 start> <T2, B, 200, 250> <T1 commit> <T3 start> <T3, C, 10, 20> — crash.
- Committed: T1 → **redo** A = 50.
- Uncommitted: T2, T3 → **undo** C = 10, B = 200 (reverse order).
- Final: A = 50, B = 200, C = 10.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · With a checkpoint
steps.body:
… <T1 commit> <checkpoint {T2}> <T2, B, 250, 300> <T4 start> <T4, D, 1, 2> <T4 commit> — crash.
- T1 committed before the checkpoint → nothing to do.
- T4 committed after → **redo** D = 2.
- T2 still active → **undo** all its changes (including those before the checkpoint).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Undoing in forward order (must be reverse).
- Ignoring transactions that were active at the checkpoint.
- Thinking deferred modification ever needs undo.

activity.prompt: Order the recovery steps for immediate modification after a crash
items: Build lists of committed and uncommitted transactions
Undo uncommitted transactions scanning the log backward
Redo committed transactions scanning the log forward
Write <T abort> records for undone transactions

quiz.q: WAL requires the log record be written
quiz.why: Write-ahead logging requires the log record for a change to be written to stable storage before the changed data page is written.
With deferred modification, changes reach the database only after commit, so nothing uncommitted is on disk, and recovery needs only redo.

quiz.q: Uncommitted transactions after a crash are
quiz.why: After a crash, transactions that hadn't committed are undone (rolled back) so the database stays consistent.
A checkpoint records a consistent point, so recovery needs to scan only the log after it, which shortens both the log and the recovery time.
ARIES recovery has three phases: analysis, redo and undo.

questions.q: Dense index has an entry for every
questions.why: A dense index has an entry for every record.

questions.q: B+ tree leaves are
questions.why: B+ tree leaves are linked in order, which supports efficient range scans and sequential access.

questions.q: WAL stands for
questions.why: WAL stands for write-ahead logging: the log is written before the data.

questions.q: Binary search on 4096 blocks costs
questions.why: 4096 = 2¹², so binary search needs about 12 block reads.

questions.q: Which supports range queries best?
questions.why: A B+ tree keeps keys in sorted, linked leaves, so range queries are efficient. Hash indexes can't do ranges.

questions.q: Immediate modification recovery needs
questions.why: With immediate modification, changes may reach disk before commit, so recovery needs undo for uncommitted ones and redo for committed ones not yet written.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A file can have many secondary indexes. Reason (R): A secondary index does not depend on the file's physical order. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: a file can have many secondary indexes. R is true and explains it: a secondary index doesn't depend on the file's physical order, so you can build one on each field.

questions.q: Block 2048 B, record 150 B: bfr
Block nested-loop: b_R = 20 (outer), b_S = 1000: transfers
questions.why: Block nested loop with outer R: read R once (20 blocks) and S once per outer block: 20 × 1000 = 20,000. Total = 20 + 20,000 = 20,020.

questions.q: Case: a reporting query filters `WHERE amount BETWEEN 1000 AND 5000` on 50 million rows. Best index?
questions.why: A range condition (BETWEEN) is best served by a B+ tree on amount, since its leaves are in order. A hash index can't do ranges.

questions.q: B+ tree: block 1024 B, key 9 B, block pointer 7 B. Internal order p:
questions.why: An internal node holds p pointers and p − 1 keys: 7p + 9(p − 1) ≤ 1024 → 16p ≤ 1033 → p = 64.

questions.q: Same, leaf with record pointer 7 B and one next pointer 7 B: q
questions.why: A leaf holds q (key + record pointer) pairs plus one next pointer: q(9 + 7) + 7 ≤ 1024 → 16q ≤ 1017 → q = 63.

questions.q: Log: <T1 start> <T1, A, 5, 10> <T1 commit> <T2 start> <T2, A, 10, 20> — crash. Value of A after recovery (immediate modification)?
questions.why: Redo committed T1 (A = 10), undo uncommitted T2 (restore old value 10) → A = 10.

questions.q: r = 2,00,000 records, 10 per block, primary index fan-out 100. Multilevel index access cost (levels + 1 data block)
questions.why: 20,000 blocks → index L1 200 blocks → L2 2 blocks → L3 1 block: 3 levels + 1 = 4.

questions.q: Extendible hashing with global depth 3 has how many directory entries?
questions.why: The directory in extendible hashing has 2^(global depth) entries: 2³ = 8.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.why: A checkpoint shortens the recovery scan. Deferred modification needs redo only, a sparse index needs sorted data, and hashing doesn't support range queries.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · DBMS
courses.summary: Formula and rule sheet for every DBMS unit, a mixed SQL + theory drill, and two mock papers as the course exam.
outcomes: Learners can recall every DBMS rule and formula
Learners can solve mixed GATE-style DBMS questions
Learners can write correct SQL under time pressure

scenes.text: Sana prints one page of DBMS rules the night before her exam.
Each rule comes with its trap.

steps.title: Modelling and algebra
steps.body:
- 1:N → FK on N side; M:N → new table; multivalued → new table; weak → owner PK + partial key
- Superkeys with single key A in n attributes: 2ⁿ⁻¹
- |R × S| = |R||S|; natural join with no common attributes = product
- R ÷ S = π_A(R) − π_A((π_A(R) × S) − R)

steps.title: SQL
steps.body:
- Order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT
- Aggregates ignore NULL (except COUNT(*)); NOT IN with NULL → empty
- Second highest: MAX(salary) WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX…)
- RANK leaves gaps, DENSE_RANK does not

steps.title: Normalization
steps.body:
- Attributes never on RHS ∈ every key
- 2NF: no partial; 3NF: X superkey or A prime; BCNF: X superkey
- Lossless: (R1 ∩ R2) → R1 or R2
- 3NF synthesis: lossless + dependency preserving; BCNF: lossless only

steps.title: Transactions and storage
steps.body:
- Conflict serializable ⇔ acyclic precedence graph
- Recoverable: writer commits before reader commits; cascadeless: no dirty reads
- 2PL ⇒ conflict serializable; not deadlock-free
- Wait–die: older waits, younger dies; wound–wait: older wounds, younger waits
- B+ internal: p·P + (p − 1)K ≤ B; leaf: q(K + Pr) + P ≤ B
- Recovery: undo uncommitted (backward), redo committed (forward)

steps.title: Top traps
steps.body:
- Superkey ≠ candidate key (check minimality)
- WHERE cannot use aggregates — use HAVING

questions.why: B never appears on a right side, so it's in every key. AB⁺ = ABCD, BC⁺ = BCDA (C → D, D → A, then AB → C), and BD⁺ = BDAC. So the keys are AB, BC and BD.

questions.why: R1(A) before W2(A) gives T1 → T2, and W2(A) before W1(A) gives T2 → T1. That's a cycle, so it isn't conflict serializable.

questions.why: An internal node has p pointers and p − 1 keys: 6p + 10(p − 1) ≤ 1024 → 16p ≤ 1034 → p = 64.

questions.why: 40,000/20 = 2000 blocks. Binary search takes ⌈log₂ 2000⌉ = 11 block reads (2¹⁰ = 1024 < 2000 ≤ 2048 = 2¹¹).

questions.why: Self-join on dept pairs each employee with every employee of the same department, including themselves. Each department has 2 employees, giving 2 × 2 = 4 pairs, and 3 departments give 12.

questions.q: [Paper B] R(A,B,C,D,E), F = {A → B, B → C, C → D, D → E}; decomposition (A,B,C), (C,D,E) is
questions.why: The common attribute C determines C, D and E, so it's a key of the second part, which makes the split lossless. A → B and B → C live in the first part, and C → D and D → E in the second, so all FDs are preserved.

steps.title: Positional value
steps.body:
A number in base **r** with digits d(n-1)…d1 d0 . d-1 d-2 has value Σ di × r^i. Binary r=2 (digits 0,1), octal r=8, decimal r=10, hex r=16 (0–9, A–F with A=10 … F=15).

An n-bit unsigned binary number represents 0 … 2^n − 1.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **1's complement** of an n-bit number: invert every bit.
- **2's complement**: 1's complement + 1 (equivalently 2^n − N).
- **Sign-magnitude**, **1's complement** and **2's complement** are the three signed representations; 2's complement is universal because it has a single zero and ordinary addition works.

n-bit 2's complement range: **−2^(n−1) … 2^(n−1) − 1** (8-bit: −128 … 127).

steps.title: Rule for signed overflow
steps.body: Overflow occurs when two operands of the **same sign** give a result of the **opposite sign**. In hardware: **V = C(n−1) XOR C(n)**, the carry into the MSB XOR the carry out of the MSB. Adding numbers of opposite signs can never overflow. For unsigned numbers, overflow = carry out of the MSB.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing carry (unsigned) with overflow (signed): 11111111 + 00000001 gives carry 1 but, as signed (−1 + 1 = 0), no overflow.
- Believing overflow can occur when adding a positive and a negative number.

statements.why: Opposite signs never overflow; result is 10.

- **Gray**: adjacent values differ in one bit. Binary→Gray: G(n−1)=B(n−1); Gi = Bi+1 ⊕ Bi. Gray→binary: B(n−1)=G(n−1); Bi = Bi+1 ⊕ Gi.

lessons.title: Boolean algebra: postulates, laws and De Morgan

steps.title: Key laws
steps.body:
- Identity A+0=A, A·1=A; Null A+1=1, A·0=0; Idempotent A+A=A; Complement A+A'=1, A·A'=0; Involution A''=A.
- Distributive: A(B+C)=AB+AC **and** A+BC=(A+B)(A+C).
- Absorption: A+AB=A, A(A+B)=A. Redundancy: A+A'B=A+B.
- **De Morgan**: (A+B)'=A'B', (AB)'=A'+B'.
- Consensus: AB+A'C+BC = AB+A'C.
- **Duality**: swap + with ·, 0 with 1 to get another valid identity.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A + A'B = (A + A')(A + B) = 1·(A+B) = **A+B**.

**Ex 2.** Simplify F = AB + A'C + BC: BC is the consensus term → F = **AB + A'C**.

**Ex 3.** F = (A+B)(A+C) = A + BC. Complement of F = A(B'+C') ... apply De Morgan: (A+BC)' = A'(B'+C') = A'B' + A'C'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing (A+B)' = A'+B' (wrong; the operator changes AND↔OR, so it is A'B').
- Forgetting that A+BC distributes as (A+B)(A+C).
- Dropping a bar when complementing a whole expression.

lessons.title: Canonical forms: minterms, maxterms, SOP and POS

scenes.text: A seat-belt alarm has a truth table written by the safety team.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- A **minterm** mi is the AND of all n variables, true for exactly one input row; a **maxterm** Mi is the OR of all n variables, false for exactly one row.
- Canonical SOP: F = Σ m(rows where F=1). Canonical POS: F = Π M(rows where F=0). Mi = (mi)'.
- F' = Σ m(rows where F=0), so Σ m(list) = Π M(complement list).
- Number of distinct Boolean functions of n variables = **2^(2^n)**.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** F(A,B,C)=Σm(1,2,4,7) is the 3-input XOR (odd parity). POS form: Π M(0,3,5,6).

**Ex 2.** Write F = A + B'C in canonical SOP: A covers 100,101,110,111 (m4–m7); B'C covers 001,101 (m1,m5). Union: Σm(1,4,5,6,7).

**Ex 3.** 2 variables → 2^4 = 16 functions; 3 variables → 2^8 = 256.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- In POS, writing the variable as complemented when its bit is 0 — for a maxterm, bit 0 → uncomplemented variable, bit 1 → complemented.
- Mixing up Σm and ΠM index lists.
- Treating don't-cares as zeros without saying so.

story.title: When the map has six variables

scenes.text: EDA tools minimise functions of dozens of variables; K-maps stop at five or six.
The tabular method is the algorithm those tools build on: find all prime implicants, then pick a minimum cover.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body:
1. List minterms (and don't-cares) in binary and group by number of 1s.
2. Combine groups whose numbers of 1s differ by one and whose binary differs in exactly one bit; mark that bit '-'. Repeat until no more combining.
3. Unchecked terms are **prime implicants**.
4. Build a prime implicant chart (don't-cares excluded from columns); select essential PIs; cover the rest with a minimum set (Petrick's method for cyclic charts).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
F(A,B,C)=Σm(0,1,2,5,6,7).
Groups: 0:000 | 1:001, 2:010 | 5:101, 6:110 | 7:111.
Pairs: 0–1 (00-) → A'B'; 0–2 (0-0) → A'C'; 1–5 (-01) → B'C; 2–6 (-10) → BC'; 5–7 (1-1) → AC; 6–7 (11-) → AB.
No quads. **6 prime implicants, none essential** (every minterm is covered twice) — a cyclic chart. Two minimum covers of 3 terms: A'B' + BC' + AC, or A'C' + B'C + AB.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

- Placing don't-cares as columns in the PI chart.
- Assuming the minimum cover is unique.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Mathematical Logic and Proofs
courses.summary: Propositions and connectives, truth tables, tautologies and logical equivalence, normal forms, predicates and quantifiers, rules of inference, and proof methods including mathematical induction.
outcomes: Learners can build truth tables and test tautologies and equivalences
Learners can convert formulas to CNF/DNF

scenes.text: A shop sign says: 'If you spend ₹2000, you get a free bag.' Tara spent ₹1500 and still got a bag. Did the shop lie?
A truth table for p → q shows the promise is only broken when p is true and q is false. The shop is honest.

steps.title: Connectives
steps.body:
A **proposition** is a statement that is true or false.
- ¬p (not), p ∧ q (and), p ∨ q (or), p ⊕ q (xor)
- **p → q** is false only when p = T and q = F
- **p ↔ q** is true when both have the same value

For p → q: converse q → p, inverse ¬p → ¬q, **contrapositive ¬q → ¬p (equivalent)**.

steps.title: Solved example: truth table
steps.body:
(p → q) ∧ (q → p):
- TT: T∧T = T
- TF: F∧T = F
- FT: T∧F = F
- FF: T∧T = T
Same as p ↔ q ✔. A formula with n variables has 2ⁿ rows.

steps.title: Solved example: tautology
steps.body:
Is (p ∧ (p → q)) → q a tautology?
- The only way to make it false: p ∧ (p → q) = T and q = F. Then p = T and p → q = T forces q = T — contradiction.
- So it is always true: **modus ponens** is a tautology.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking p → q is false when p is false.
- Treating the converse as equivalent to the original.
- Reading 'p unless q' wrongly: it means ¬q → p, i.e. p ∨ q.
- 'p only if q' means p → q, not q → p.

steps.title: Precedence
steps.body: ¬ binds tightest, then ∧, ∨, →, ↔. p → q → r is read p → (q → r).

activity.prompt: Print the truth table of p → q as four lines in the order TT, TF, FT, FF, each line like `T T T` (p q result).

F T T
