Mock B1. Assertion: K₅ is not planar. Reason: K₅ has 10 > 3·5 − 6 edges.
questions.why: K₅ has 10 edges, but a simple planar graph with 5 vertices can have at most 3·5 − 6 = 9. So K₅ is not planar, and the edge bound is the reason.

questions.q: Mock B2. Number of surjections from a 4-set onto a 3-set
questions.why: By inclusion–exclusion, surjections 4→3 = 3⁴ − 3·2⁴ + 3·1⁴ = 81 − 48 + 3 = 36.

questions.q: Mock B3. In a group, (ab)⁻¹ =
questions.why: In a group, (ab)(b⁻¹a⁻¹) = a(bb⁻¹)a⁻¹ = e. So (ab)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a⁻¹, with the order reversed.

questions.q: Mock B4. Case: 50 students each pick one of 7 electives. At least how many students must share some elective?
questions.why: By the pigeonhole principle, some elective gets at least ⌈50/7⌉ = 8 students, since 7·7 = 49 < 50.

questions.q: Mock B5. χ(K_{3,3})
questions.why: K_{3,3} is bipartite, so two colours suffice (one per side). It has edges, so one colour is not enough: χ = 2.

questions.q: Mock B6. Which statement is valid? 'All CSE students code. Riya does not code.'
options: Riya is not a CSE student
Some CSE students do not code
questions.why: From All CSE students code, a non-coder cannot be a CSE student (contrapositive, modus tollens). It does not follow that some CSE students do not code.

questions.q: Mock B7. Transitive closure of {(1,2),(2,3),(3,4)} on {1,2,3,4} has pairs
questions.why: Chains give (1,3), (2,4), and (1,4). Together with the original 3 pairs this is 6 pairs.

questions.q: Mock B8. Number of edges in a 4-regular graph on 9 vertices
questions.why: The degree sum is 9·4 = 36 and equals 2E, so E = 18.

questions.q: Mock B9. Coefficient of x²y³ in (x + 2y)⁵
questions.why: By the binomial theorem the x²y³ term has coefficient C(5,2)·2³ = 10·8 = 80.

questions.q: Mock B10. Order of 3 in (ℤ₇*, × mod 7)
questions.why: Powers of 3 mod 7 are 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1, so 3⁶ ≡ 1 first at exponent 6. Hence the order is 6 (3 is a primitive root).

uni-cse-distributed.title: Distributed Systems (B.Tech)
uni-cse-distributed.description: A full distributed-systems course: models and architectures, time and ordering, coordination, consensus and fault tolerance, replication and consistency, distributed file systems, transactions and partitioning, with Python simulations and a practical/viva revision unit.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Introduction, models and architectures
courses.summary: What a distributed system is, its goals (transparency, openness, scalability), common architectures, system and failure models, availability arithmetic, RPC and Amdahl's law, with worked numericals and code labs.
outcomes: Define a distributed system and list the eight fallacies
Identify the types of transparency
Compare client-server, multi-tier, peer-to-peer and microservice architectures
Compute availability of series and parallel components
Explain RPC and speedup limits

lessons.title: What is a distributed system? Goals and transparency

scenes.text: Sana books a ticket on her phone. Her request touches an authentication service, a seat inventory in another city and a payment gateway run by a bank.
To her it feels like one application. That illusion of unity is the main goal of a distributed system.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: A **distributed system** is a collection of autonomous computers that communicate only by passing messages over a network and appear to users as a single coherent system. Key properties: **concurrency** of components, **no global clock**, **independent failures**. Examples: web search, online banking, cloud storage, multiplayer games.

steps.title: Goals
steps.body:
- **Resource sharing** (files, printers, services).
- **Transparency**: access (hide data representation), location, migration, relocation, replication, concurrency, failure.
- **Openness**: standard interfaces and protocols.
- **Scalability**: size (more users), geography, administration. Techniques: replication, caching, partitioning, asynchronous communication.

steps.title: Fallacies of distributed computing
steps.body: Developers wrongly assume: the network is reliable; latency is zero; bandwidth is infinite; the network is secure; topology does not change; there is one administrator; transport cost is zero; the network is homogeneous.

steps.title: Which transparency?
steps.body: You open a shared file without knowing which server holds it: **location transparency**. The system hides the crash of one replica and continues: **failure transparency**. Two users edit different files with no interference: **concurrency transparency**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a multi-threaded program on one machine a distributed system (it shares memory).
- Thinking full transparency is always achievable: network latency and failures cannot be fully hidden.

activity.prompt: Match each transparency to what it hides.
pairs: Differences in data representation and how a resource is accessed
Where the resource is physically placed
Movement of a resource to another place
That several copies of a resource exist
That a component failed and recovered

quiz.why: No shared memory between nodes.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the fallacies?
quiz.why: Latency is non-zero is the truth; 'latency is zero' is the fallacy.

quiz.q: Hiding that data is replicated is
quiz.why: By definition.

quiz.q: Scaling technique that stores copies near users
quiz.why: Reduces latency and load.

lessons.title: Architectural styles: client-server, multi-tier, P2P and microservices

story.title: From one server to thousands of services

scenes.text: A shop starts with one server running everything. Black Friday crashes it.
The team splits it into web, application and database tiers, later into microservices behind an API gateway.

steps.title: Styles
steps.body:
- **Client-server**: clients request, servers respond; simple, server is bottleneck/single point of failure.
- **Multi-tier (n-tier)**: presentation, application logic, data, each independently scalable.
- **Peer-to-peer**: all nodes are both client and server; no central point; scales with participants; examples BitTorrent, DHTs (Chord, Kademlia).
- **Microservices**: small independently deployable services communicating via APIs/messages.
- **Event-driven / publish-subscribe**: decoupled through a broker.

steps.title: Middleware
steps.body: Middleware sits between OS and applications offering RPC/RMI, message queues, naming and transactions. Layers: application, middleware, OS, hardware.

steps.title: Trade-off analysis
steps.body: Messaging app: central server = easy moderation and search but a bottleneck and single point of failure; pure P2P = resilient and cheap but harder to search, secure and keep consistent. Many real systems are **hybrid** (supernodes).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling microservices free: they add network failures, tracing and data-consistency problems.
- Confusing physical 'tier' (machine) with logical 'layer'.

steps.title: Models
steps.body: **Synchronous**: known bounds on message delay, clock drift and process speed. **Asynchronous**: no bounds; cannot tell a slow node from a dead one (the root of the FLP result). **Partially synchronous**: bounds exist but are unknown or hold eventually - the practical model.

steps.title: Failure types
steps.body:
- **Crash (fail-stop)**: halts and stays halted.
- **Omission**: send/receive omissions (lost messages).
- **Timing**: response outside the bound.
- **Byzantine (arbitrary)**: wrong or malicious behaviour.
Network **partition** splits nodes into groups that cannot talk.

steps.title: Availability
steps.body: A = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR). **Series** (all needed): A = A1 x A2. **Parallel** (any one suffices, independent): A = 1 - (1-A1)(1-A2)...

steps.title: Solved: series
steps.body: Web (99%) and database (99%) in series: 0.99 x 0.99 = 0.9801 = **98.01%** (about 7.3 days of downtime a year).

steps.title: Solved: parallel
steps.body: Two replicas of 99% each: 1 - 0.01^2 = **99.99%**. Three replicas of 90% each: 1 - 0.1^3 = 99.9%.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Assuming replicas fail independently: a shared power feed or software bug fails them together, so real availability is lower.

lessons.title: Lab: Remote Procedure Call - stubs and marshalling

story.title: Calling a function on another computer

scenes.text: A mobile app calls getBalance(account) as if it were local. The call actually crosses the network.
Hidden stubs pack the arguments into bytes, send them, and unpack the reply.

steps.title: How RPC works
steps.body:
1. The client calls the **client stub**, which **marshals** (serialises) the arguments.
2. The message is sent to the server; the **server stub** unmarshals it and calls the real procedure.
3. The result travels back the same way.
An **IDL** (interface definition language) describes the interface; formats include JSON, Protocol Buffers (gRPC), XML.

steps.title: Semantics
steps.body:
- **At-least-once**: retry until reply: may execute many times (fine for idempotent calls like reading).
- **At-most-once**: duplicates filtered using request IDs: may execute zero times.
- **Exactly-once**: practically unachievable without idempotency plus de-duplication.
Use idempotency keys for payments.

steps.title: What you will build
steps.body: A tiny in-process RPC: the client builds a JSON request {id, method, params}; the server looks the method up in a registry, executes it and returns JSON {id, result}.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Passing pointers or local objects: they mean nothing on another machine.
- Not setting timeouts: the caller hangs forever on a failed server.
- Retrying non-idempotent operations (double-charging).

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone - speedup, Amdahl's law and scalability

story.title: Will 100 servers make it 100 times faster?

scenes.text: A team parallelises a report job. 90% of the work can run in parallel; 10% (merging) cannot.
They buy 10 machines and are disappointed. Amdahl's law explains why.

steps.title: Amdahl's law
steps.body: If a fraction p of work can be parallelised across N workers: **S(N) = 1 / ((1 - p) + p/N)**. As N -> infinity, S -> 1/(1-p). With p = 0.9 the maximum speedup is 10, however many machines you buy.

steps.title: Related ideas
steps.body: **Gustafson's law**: if the problem size grows with N, speedup is (1-p) + pN - large jobs scale better. **Scale up** (bigger machine) vs **scale out** (more machines). Coordination overhead (network, locks, stragglers) adds a term that Amdahl ignores.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Using p for the whole program when only the compute loop is parallel; measure it first.

activity.prompt: Compute the Amdahl speedup for p = 0.9 with N = 10 workers and print it rounded to 2 decimals.

activity.solution:

courses.title: Unit 2 · Communication, time and ordering of events
courses.summary: Message ordering and multicast, physical clock synchronisation (Cristian, Berkeley, NTP), Lamport logical clocks and vector clocks, with worked examples and code labs.
outcomes: Distinguish FIFO, causal and total ordering
Synchronise clocks with Cristian's and Berkeley's algorithms
Assign Lamport timestamps and vector timestamps
Decide whether two events are causally related or concurrent

scenes.text: In a group chat, Asha's reply 'Yes!' appears before Ravi's question 'Coming tonight?' on Meena's phone.
Messages took different paths and arrived out of order. Ordering guarantees fix this.

steps.title: Communication primitives
steps.body: **Synchronous** send blocks until delivery; **asynchronous** send returns at once (buffered). **Transient** communication loses messages if the receiver is down; **persistent** (message queues) stores them. Sockets give TCP (reliable stream) and UDP (datagrams). **Multicast** sends one message to a group.

steps.title: Ordering guarantees
steps.body:
- **FIFO order**: messages from one sender are delivered in the order sent.
- **Causal order**: if send(m1) happened-before send(m2), every process delivers m1 before m2.
- **Total order**: all processes deliver all messages in the same order (may not respect causality).
- **Reliable multicast**: if one correct process delivers m, all do (atomic delivery).
FIFO is weaker than causal; causal+total is the strongest practical ordering.

steps.title: Chat example
steps.body: Ravi asks (m1). Asha replies after reading m1 (m2). Causal order forces everyone to see m1 before m2. Without it Meena may see the reply first. Total order alone would only force everyone to agree on *some* order, which could still be m2 before m1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming TCP gives ordering across different connections.
- Equating 'reliable' with 'ordered'.

activity.prompt: Which ordering guarantee is described?

A reply is never shown before the message it answers

Used to keep replicated databases applying updates identically

lessons.title: Physical clocks: Cristian's and Berkeley algorithms

scenes.text: A bank's two servers log transactions with timestamps, but the clocks disagree by 4 seconds.
An auditor cannot decide which payment came first.

steps.title: Why clocks drift
steps.body: Quartz clocks drift by about 10^-6 (1 us per second, ~86 ms/day). There is no global clock, so nodes synchronise periodically against a reference such as UTC.

steps.title: Cristian's algorithm
steps.body: Client asks a time server at T0, receives time T_s at T1. RTT = T1 - T0. Set client time = **T_s + RTT/2**. Error is at most +/- (RTT/2 - min one-way delay).

steps.title: Solved: Cristian
steps.body: Request sent at client time 10.000 s, reply received at 10.200 s: RTT = 0.2 s. Server says 15.100 s. New client time = 15.100 + 0.100 = **15.200 s**. Error bound at most +/- 0.1 s.

steps.title: Berkeley algorithm
steps.body: A coordinator polls all machines, computes the **average** of their clock differences (ignoring outliers), and sends each machine the **adjustment** (not an absolute time, to avoid transit delay).

steps.title: Solved: Berkeley
steps.body: Master 3:00, A 3:25, B 2:50. Differences from master: 0, +25, -10. Average = +5 min. Adjustments: master +5, A -20, B +15. All become 3:05.

steps.title: NTP
steps.body: Hierarchical servers in **strata** (stratum 0 = atomic/GPS reference). Uses multiple samples, offset and delay: offset = ((t2-t1)+(t3-t4))/2. Clocks are slewed (gradually adjusted) so time never runs backward.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Setting a clock backwards abruptly (breaks logs and timers).
- Believing NTP gives microsecond accuracy over the public internet (typically milliseconds).

activity.prompt: Client sends at 10.000 s and receives the reply at 10.200 s. The server timestamp is 15.100 s. By Cristian's algorithm the new client time (seconds) is?

scenes.text: Two bank branches record 'deposit' and 'withdraw' for the same account. The wall clocks cannot say which came first, but the message from one to the other can.
Lamport (1978) showed we only need an order consistent with causality.

steps.title: Happened-before
steps.body: a -> b if (1) a and b are in the same process and a occurs first, (2) a is the send of a message and b is its receive, or (3) transitively. Events not related are **concurrent** (a || b).

steps.title: Lamport clock rules
steps.body:
Each process keeps counter C.
1. Before each local event or send: **C = C + 1** (send carries C).
2. On receive of timestamp ts: **C = max(C, ts) + 1**.
Property: a -> b implies C(a) < C(b). The converse is false: C(a) < C(b) does not imply a -> b. Break ties with process ids for a total order.

steps.title: Trace
steps.body: P1: local (C=1), send m1 (2). P2: local (1), receive m1: max(1,2)+1 = 3, send m2 (4). P1: receive m2: max(2,4)+1 = 5. Final clocks P1 = 5, P2 = 4.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not incrementing after the max on receive.
- Concluding concurrency from equal timestamps or causality from smaller ones: use vector clocks for that.

lessons.title: Lab: Vector clocks and detecting concurrency

scenes.text: Two people edit the same shared note offline and sync later.
The server must decide: was one edit based on the other, or are they conflicting? Vector clocks answer exactly this.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
Each of N processes keeps a vector V[1..N]. Local event or send at process i: **V[i] += 1**. On receive of vector W: **V = max(V, W) elementwise, then V[i] += 1**.
Compare: V <= W if every component <=; V < W if V <= W and V != W (happened-before); if neither V <= W nor W <= V the events are **concurrent**. Exactly captures causality (unlike Lamport).

steps.title: Trace
steps.body: P1 event a: [1,0,0]. P2 event b: [0,1,0] -> concurrent. P1 sends: [2,0,0]. P2 receives: max([0,1,0],[2,0,0]) = [2,1,0], then +1 own: [2,2,0]. [2,0,0] < [2,2,0] so the send happened-before the receive.

steps.title: Where used
steps.body: Dynamo-style stores, Riak and CRDT systems use version vectors to detect conflicting writes.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Vector size grows with the number of processes; real systems prune or use dotted version vectors.

activity.prompt: Write cmp(a,b) returning 'before', 'after', 'equal' or 'concurrent' for two vector clocks and print the results for the two pairs.

    ge=all(x>=y for x,y in zip(a,b))
    # decide using le and ge
    return 'equal'
print(cmp([1,0,0],[0,1,0]),cmp([2,0,0],[2,2,0]))
activity.solution:
def cmp(a,b):
    le=all(x<=y for x,y in zip(a,b))
    ge=all(x>=y for x,y in zip(a,b))
    if le and ge: return 'equal'
    if le: return 'before'
    if ge: return 'after'
    return 'concurrent'

courses.title: Unit 3 · Coordination: mutual exclusion, election, global state and deadlock
courses.summary: Distributed mutual exclusion (centralised, Ricart-Agrawala, token ring), leader election (bully, ring), global snapshots (Chandy-Lamport) and distributed deadlock detection, with message-count numericals and code labs.
outcomes: Compare mutual-exclusion algorithms by message cost and failure behaviour
Run the bully and ring election algorithms
Explain consistent cuts and the Chandy-Lamport snapshot

scenes.text: Ten offices share a single remote high-speed printer. Two jobs interleaved on the same page would be gibberish.
Only one process may be in the critical section at a time, with no central lock manager if possible.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.body: **Safety**: at most one process in the critical section (CS). **Liveness**: every request is eventually granted (no deadlock, no starvation). **Fairness**: requests granted in happened-before order.

steps.title: Algorithms
steps.body:
- **Centralised**: coordinator grants a token; 3 messages per entry (request, grant, release); single point of failure.
- **Ricart-Agrawala** (distributed, Lamport timestamps): broadcast request(ts,id) to N-1 others; enter after N-1 replies; defer replies if you are in the CS or have an earlier request. **2(N-1) messages** per entry.
- **Token ring**: a token circulates; whoever holds it may enter. 1 to N-1 messages per entry (token passing continues even when idle); token loss must be detected.
- **Maekawa** (voting sets of size about sqrt(N)): ~3 sqrt(N) messages; deadlock possible.

steps.title: Solved: message count
steps.body: N = 6 processes. Ricart-Agrawala: 2 x 5 = **10 messages** per CS entry. Centralised: 3. Token ring: up to 5.

steps.title: Solved: tie-breaking
steps.body: Requests (ts=8, P2) and (ts=8, P3): equal timestamps, so the lower process id has priority. P3 replies to P2 at once; P2 defers its reply to P3 until it leaves the CS. P2 enters first.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming Ricart-Agrawala tolerates failures: a crashed process never replies, blocking everyone.
- Forgetting that timestamps need the Lamport clock rule on message receipt.

activity.prompt: In a system of N = 6 processes, how many messages does one critical-section entry cost with the Ricart-Agrawala algorithm?

steps.title: Rules for receiving request(ts,j) at process i
steps.body:
- If i is not interested and not in the CS: reply immediately.
- If i is in the CS: defer the reply (queue it).
- If i also wants the CS: compare (ts_i, i) with (ts_j, j); if the incoming request is **smaller (earlier)**, reply now; otherwise defer.
On leaving the CS reply to all deferred requests.

steps.title: Outcome
steps.body: P3 (idle) replies to both. P1 and P2 compare: P1 (5) < P2 (7), so P2 replies to P1 and P1 defers P2. P1 gets 2 replies and enters. On exit P1 sends the deferred reply to P2; P2 now has 2 replies and enters. Messages: each requester sends 2 requests and receives 2 replies = 4 = 2(N-1) per entry, so 8 messages for the two entries.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Replying to an earlier request while in the CS: it would break safety.

lessons.title: Lab: Leader election - bully and ring algorithms

scenes.text: The coordinator of a database cluster stops responding at 3 AM.
The remaining nodes must agree on a new leader without human help.

steps.title: Bully algorithm
steps.body: Assumes every process knows all ids. A process P that notices the coordinator is dead sends ELECTION to all processes with **higher ids**. If none answers, P wins and broadcasts COORDINATOR. If a higher one answers OK, P stops and that process starts its own election. The highest live id always wins ('bullies' the rest). Worst case O(N^2) messages.

steps.title: Ring algorithm
steps.body: Processes form a logical ring. The initiator sends ELECTION carrying its id around the ring; each process appends its own id. When the message returns to the initiator it picks the highest id and circulates a COORDINATOR message. About 2N messages per election (N for election, N for announcement).

steps.title: Solved
steps.body: Processes 1..5, 5 crashed. P2 starts: sends to 3, 4; both answer OK; P3 and P4 start elections; P3 contacts 4 (and 5, no answer); P4 contacts only 5 (dead), gets no reply, **P4 wins**, broadcasts COORDINATOR.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Not handling a recovered high-id process: in bully a restarted highest id immediately takes over.

activity.prompt: Implement the bully election: alive nodes are [1,2,3,4] (5 crashed). Process 2 starts the election. Print the winner.
activity.starter:
alive=[1,2,3,4]
def election(p):
    higher=[q for q in alive if q>p]
    # if nobody higher: p wins; else the highest answering process continues
    return p
print(election(2))
activity.hint: if not higher: return p; else return election(min(higher))

lessons.title: Global state and the Chandy-Lamport snapshot

scenes.text: A bank wants the total balance across two branches at an instant, but transfers are in flight in the network.
If it reads the branches at different moments it may count a transfer twice or not at all.

steps.title: Consistent cuts
steps.body: A **cut** is a set of events, one prefix per process. It is **consistent** if for every receive in the cut, the matching send is also in the cut (no message received 'from the future'). A **global state** = local states + messages in transit on the channels.

steps.title: Chandy-Lamport (FIFO channels)
steps.body:
1. The initiator records its state and sends a **marker** on every outgoing channel.
2. On first receiving a marker on channel c: record own state, mark channel c's state as **empty**, and send markers on all outgoing channels; start recording messages arriving on other channels.
3. On a marker on another channel d: stop recording; the messages recorded on d are its channel state.
The snapshot terminates when all processes have received markers on all incoming channels. Cost: one marker per channel.

steps.title: Solved: invariant
steps.body: A and B hold 400 and 350 recorded locally; the recorded channel A->B holds a transfer of 50 in flight. Total = 400 + 350 + 50 = **800**, the same as the true total (800) because the snapshot is consistent.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Needing synchronised clocks: the algorithm is clock-free.
- Assuming the snapshot equals a state that really existed at one instant: it is a state that **could** have occurred (reachable), enough for stable properties like deadlock or termination.

activity.prompt: Recorded states: A = 400, B = 350, and the channel A->B recorded a message transferring 50. What total does the snapshot report?

options: A send is in the cut but not its receive
A receive is in the cut but its send is not

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone - deadlock detection with a wait-for graph

story.title: Three tasks waiting in a circle

scenes.text: Task A holds lock 1 and wants lock 2 on another server. Task B holds 2, wants 3. Task C holds 3, wants 1.
Nobody can proceed. A monitor builds a wait-for graph and finds the cycle.

steps.title: Wait-for graph (WFG)
steps.body: Nodes are processes; edge P -> Q means P waits for a resource held by Q. In a single-instance resource system **a cycle = deadlock**. In distributed systems each site has a local WFG; a **global** WFG is the union and may contain a cycle no site sees alone.

steps.title: Approaches
steps.body:
- **Centralised**: sites send WFG edges to a coordinator (risk of **phantom deadlocks** from stale edges).
- **Distributed (edge chasing, Chandy-Misra-Haas)**: a blocked process sends a probe (initiator, sender, receiver); if the initiator receives its own probe, a cycle exists.
- **Prevention** (ordering resources, wait-die / wound-wait with timestamps) and **timeouts** (simple, with false positives).

steps.title: Solved
steps.body: Graph {1:[2], 2:[3], 3:[1]} has a cycle 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 1: deadlock. Graph {1:[2], 2:[3], 3:[]} has none: P3 will finish and release.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Killing every process in the cycle: abort the cheapest victim (lowest priority/work done) to break it.

lessons.title: Atomic commit: two-phase and three-phase commit

scenes.text: Rahul transfers Rs 5,000 from Bank A to Bank B. A debits, B credits.
If A debits and then B's server crashes, the money vanishes. Both must commit or both abort.

steps.title: Goal
steps.body: **Atomic commitment**: all participants commit a distributed transaction or all abort. Requires logging to stable storage before replying so decisions survive crashes.

steps.title: Two-phase commit (2PC)
steps.body:
**Phase 1 (voting)**: coordinator sends PREPARE; each participant force-writes a log record and replies **VOTE-COMMIT** (it promises it can commit) or **VOTE-ABORT**.
**Phase 2 (decision)**: if all voted commit, coordinator logs and sends **GLOBAL-COMMIT**; otherwise **GLOBAL-ABORT**. Participants act and ACK.
Cost: 4 messages per participant (prepare, vote, decision, ack).

steps.title: Blocking problem
steps.body: If the coordinator crashes after participants voted commit, they are **uncertain**: they cannot decide alone and hold locks until the coordinator recovers. **3PC** adds a PRE-COMMIT phase so participants can elect a new coordinator and proceed (non-blocking under crash failures with no partitions), but costs an extra round and is rarely used; modern systems prefer Paxos-based commit.

steps.title: Solved: message count
steps.body: 1 coordinator, 4 participants: prepare 4 + votes 4 + decisions 4 + acks 4 = **16 messages**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Voting commit before logging: after a crash the promise is forgotten.
- Thinking 2PC solves consensus on failure of the coordinator: it blocks.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of a successful two-phase commit.

scenes.text: A coordinator keeps a log of votes. Any missing or negative vote forces an abort.

steps.title: Decision rule
steps.body: The coordinator commits only if **every** participant answered VOTE-COMMIT within the timeout. A missing vote (crashed or slow) is treated as abort - safe because nothing has been committed yet.

steps.title: Cases
steps.body: [commit, commit, commit] -> COMMIT. [commit, commit, abort] -> ABORT. [commit, None, commit] (None = timeout) -> ABORT.

steps.title: Participant rule
steps.body: After voting commit a participant must wait for the decision; it may query other participants (cooperative termination) if the coordinator is silent.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Treating a timeout after voting commit as abort at the participant: unsafe, the coordinator may have decided to commit.

lessons.title: Consensus, FLP, Paxos and Byzantine faults

scenes.text: Five replicas of a configuration service must agree on the next leader. Messages may be delayed and nodes may crash.
This is the consensus problem - the heart of reliable distributed systems.

steps.title: Consensus
steps.body: Processes propose values; they must satisfy **Agreement** (no two decide differently), **Validity** (the decided value was proposed) and **Termination** (every correct process eventually decides). **FLP impossibility (1985)**: in a purely asynchronous system, no deterministic algorithm can guarantee consensus if even one process may crash. Practical systems sacrifice guaranteed termination (use timeouts/leaders/randomisation) but never safety.

steps.title: Paxos (single decree)
steps.body: Roles: proposers, acceptors, learners. **Phase 1**: proposer picks a unique number n, sends PREPARE(n); acceptors promise not to accept lower numbers and report any value already accepted. **Phase 2**: proposer sends ACCEPT(n, v) where v is the value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal reported, else its own; acceptors accept unless they promised higher. A value is **chosen** when a **majority** accepts it. Majority = floor(N/2) + 1, so any two majorities intersect, which preserves safety. It tolerates f crash failures with N = 2f + 1.

steps.title: Byzantine faults
steps.body: With arbitrary (malicious) behaviour, agreement needs **N >= 3f + 1** nodes to tolerate f faulty (Lamport-Shostak-Pease). PBFT achieves this with 3 message phases. Blockchains use related ideas (proof-of-work, PoS) in open networks.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body: 7 acceptors: majority = 4; tolerates 3 crashes. For Byzantine tolerance of f = 2 you need N >= 7. With N = 10 nodes the maximum f = floor((10-1)/3) = 3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing FLP says consensus is impossible in practice: it says no *guarantee* without timing assumptions.
- Using even cluster sizes: 4 nodes tolerate 1 crash, the same as 3.

lessons.title: Lab: Raft - elections, log replication and the commit index

scenes.text: In an etcd-style cluster the leader receives every write and replicates it to followers.
A write is committed once a majority has stored it.

steps.title: Raft in one page
steps.body: Nodes are **follower**, **candidate** or **leader**; time is divided into **terms**. A follower that hears no heartbeat within a randomised **election timeout** (e.g. 150-300 ms) becomes a candidate, increments the term, votes for itself and requests votes; a majority makes it leader. Each node votes at most once per term, and only for a candidate whose log is at least as up-to-date. The leader appends client commands to its log, sends **AppendEntries** (also used as heartbeat), and advances the **commitIndex** to the highest index stored on a majority (whose entry is from the current term). Followers apply committed entries in order.

steps.title: Solved: commit index
steps.body: Match indices (highest replicated entry) for 5 nodes including the leader: [5, 3, 4, 5, 2]. Sorted ascending: [2,3,4,5,5]. A majority (3 nodes) have at least index 4, so **commitIndex = 4**: it is the 3rd largest value.

steps.title: Why randomised timeouts
steps.body: They make split votes rare: usually one node times out first and wins before others start.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Committing entries from earlier terms just by counting replicas (Raft requires a current-term entry to be replicated).
- Forgetting the leader counts itself in the majority.

activity.solution:

commit=sorted(match)[(n-1)//2]
print(commit)
activity.hint: sorted(match)[(n-1)//2]

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone - heartbeats and failure detection

story.title: Who is dead and who is just slow?

scenes.text: Each node sends a heartbeat every 5 seconds. Node C has not been heard from for 30 seconds.
A timeout detector suspects C. In an asynchronous network it can never be sure.

steps.title: Failure detectors
steps.body: A **failure detector** reports suspected nodes. Properties: **completeness** (crashed nodes are eventually suspected) and **accuracy** (correct nodes are not suspected). With asynchrony you cannot have both perfectly, so practical detectors use timeouts or adaptive methods such as the **phi accrual** detector (used in Cassandra and Akka), which outputs a suspicion level instead of yes/no.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body: Last heartbeat times: A at 100 s, B at 92 s, C at 70 s; now = 100 s; timeout = 15 s. Silent for: A 0, B 8, C 30. Only **C** exceeds 15 s and is suspected.

steps.title: Choosing the timeout
steps.body: Too short = false positives (unnecessary failovers); too long = slow recovery. Gossip protocols (SWIM) spread suspicion to reduce false alarms.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Treating 'suspected' as 'dead' and starting a second leader: use leases/fencing tokens so a wrongly suspected leader cannot corrupt state.

story.title: The shopping cart that never loses an item

scenes.text: An online store keeps each customer's cart on three servers in different cities.
If one fails the cart survives, and customers near each city read locally. But all three copies must be kept in step.

steps.title: Reasons
steps.body: **Reliability/availability** (survive failures), **performance** (serve reads near users, spread load), **scalability**. The price: keeping copies **consistent**.

steps.title: Architectures
steps.body:
- **Primary-backup (passive)**: clients talk to the primary; it forwards updates to backups. Failover promotes a backup. Simple; synchronous replication is safe but slow, asynchronous may lose the last updates.
- **Active replication / replicated state machine**: all replicas execute the same deterministic commands in the same total order (via consensus). No failover pause.
- **Chain replication**: writes enter at the head and pass down the chain; reads go to the tail; strong consistency with high throughput.
- **Multi-leader** and **leaderless** (Dynamo style) allow writes at several nodes; conflicts must be resolved.

steps.title: Synchronous vs asynchronous
steps.body: Primary replicates to 2 backups. Synchronous: acknowledge the client after both ACK: latency = slowest backup, no data loss on primary crash. Asynchronous: acknowledge immediately: lowest latency, but updates not yet shipped are lost on failover.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Replication is not backup: a bad delete is replicated to every copy.
- Reading from an asynchronous replica and expecting your own write (stale read).

statements.s: Replication can improve both availability and read performance.
statements.why: Copies survive failures and serve nearby reads.

statements.s: Asynchronous primary-backup can lose acknowledged writes on failover.
statements.why: Updates not yet shipped are missing on the backup.

statements.s: Replication replaces the need for backups.
In chain replication, reads are served by the tail.
statements.why: The tail holds only fully replicated writes.

scenes.text: Dev uploads a photo on his phone and instantly opens the album on his laptop. It is missing.
A few seconds later it appears. The system chose speed over immediate agreement.

steps.title: The spectrum (strong to weak)
steps.body:
- **Linearizability (strong/atomic)**: each operation appears to take effect instantly at some point between its start and end; behaves like one copy. Needs coordination.
- **Sequential consistency**: all processes see one common order consistent with each process's program order (not necessarily real time).
- **Causal consistency**: causally related writes seen in order everywhere; concurrent writes may differ.
- **Eventual consistency**: if updates stop, all replicas converge. Typical of DNS and Dynamo-style stores.
**Client-centric guarantees**: read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes-follow-reads.

steps.title: Example
steps.body: x = 0 initially. P1 writes x = 1, then P2 reads x = 0 after P1's write completed (in real time). Linearizability forbids this; sequential consistency allows it (P2's read can be ordered earlier); eventual consistency allows it temporarily.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing database ACID 'consistency' (constraints hold) with replica consistency.
- Assuming eventual consistency means 'never consistent': it guarantees convergence, not when.

scenes.text: A key-value store keeps N = 5 copies. A write must be acknowledged by W replicas; a read asks R replicas.
If R + W > N the read set and the last write set must overlap, so a read sees the newest value.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- **R + W > N**: read and write quorums intersect: reads see the latest write (strong-ish, with versions/timestamps to pick the newest).
- **W > N/2**: two writes cannot both succeed on disjoint sets, avoiding conflicting writes.
- Latency/availability trade: W = N (writes slow, survives no failure), R = 1 (reads fast). Dynamo/Cassandra let you tune per request (e.g. QUORUM = floor(N/2)+1).

steps.title: Solved
steps.body: N = 5. (R=3,W=3): 6 > 5 yes. (R=2,W=3): 5 > 5 no - a read may miss the latest write. For W = 3, the minimum R for overlap is N - W + 1 = **3**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing R + W > N gives linearizability: sloppy quorums, hinted handoff and clock-based conflict resolution can still return stale data.
- Forgetting that failed replicas reduce the available quorum.

lessons.title: CAP theorem, PACELC and design trade-offs

scenes.text: A fibre cut separates a bank's Mumbai and Chennai data centres. Both can still reach customers but not each other.
Should they keep serving (risking diverging balances) or refuse some requests (staying correct but unavailable)?

steps.title: CAP (Brewer; proved by Gilbert and Lynch)
steps.body: A distributed data store cannot simultaneously provide all three of **Consistency** (linearizability), **Availability** (every non-failed node answers every request) and **Partition tolerance**. Since partitions happen, the real choice during a partition is **CP** (refuse/stall to stay consistent) or **AP** (answer, possibly stale, reconcile later). When there is no partition you can have both C and A.

steps.title: PACELC
steps.body: If **P**artition: choose **A**vailability or **C**onsistency; **E**lse (normal operation): choose **L**atency or **C**onsistency. Explains why even healthy systems trade consistency for lower latency (e.g. asynchronous replication).

steps.title: Design choices
steps.body:
- A shopping cart or social feed: AP, merge later (CRDTs, last-writer-wins).
- A bank ledger or seat booking for the last seat: CP; better to return an error than to double-spend.
- Coordination services (ZooKeeper, etcd): CP, they favour consistency.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 'pick any two of three': partition tolerance is not optional.

steps.title: CRDTs
steps.body: A **conflict-free replicated data type** has a merge function that is **commutative, associative and idempotent**, so replicas converge regardless of message order or duplication. Two styles: state-based (CvRDT: merge full state) and operation-based (CmRDT).

steps.title: G-Counter
steps.body: Grow-only counter: each replica i has its own slot. Increment adds to its own slot only. **merge = element-wise max**; **value = sum of slots**. A **PN-Counter** uses two G-Counters (increments and decrements). Others: G-Set, OR-Set (add/remove), LWW-Register (last-writer-wins by timestamp, may drop concurrent updates), sequence CRDTs for collaborative text editing.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body: Replica A: {A:3, B:0}; replica B: {A:2, B:4}. Merge = {A:3, B:4}. Value = **7**. Merging again or in the other order gives the same result (idempotent, commutative).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Merging with sum instead of max: duplicated messages double count.
- Expecting an arbitrary data type (e.g. a bank balance with a floor of zero) to be a CRDT: invariants need coordination.

lessons.title: Distributed file systems: NFS, AFS and GFS/HDFS

story.title: A 1 GB file across a cluster

scenes.text: An analytics team uploads a 1,000 MB log file to a cluster. No single disk should hold all of it, and losing a server must not lose data.
The file system splits it into blocks and keeps several copies.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.body: Transparency (access/location), performance (caching), fault tolerance (replication), consistency semantics, scalability, security.

steps.title: NFS and AFS
steps.body: **NFS** (Sun): client-server, remote procedure calls; NFSv2/v3 servers are **stateless** (each request self-contained, so crash recovery is simple, but no locking in the protocol); clients cache with periodic validation (close-to-open consistency in practice). **AFS** (Andrew): whole-file caching on the client's disk with **callbacks** (server promises to notify when the file changes); better scalability, **session semantics** (changes visible to others when the file is closed).

steps.title: GFS and HDFS
steps.body: Designed for huge files, streaming reads and appends on commodity hardware where failure is normal. **Master/NameNode** keeps metadata (file -> blocks -> locations) in memory; **chunk servers/DataNodes** store large blocks (GFS 64 MB chunks; HDFS default **128 MB** blocks) replicated (default factor **3**, rack-aware). Clients get locations from the master and then talk to data servers directly, so the master is not a data bottleneck. A standby NameNode and journal nodes remove the single point of failure in HDFS HA.

steps.title: Solved: blocks and storage
steps.body: File 1,000 MB, block 128 MB: ceil(1000/128) = **8 blocks** (7 full + one of 104 MB). With replication 3 the raw storage used is 3 x 1,000 = 3,000 MB (HDFS stores the last block at its actual size).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using HDFS for millions of tiny files: the NameNode keeps metadata for each in RAM.
- Assuming NFS/AFS give POSIX-like instant consistency across clients.

activity.prompt: An HDFS cluster uses a 128 MB block size. How many blocks does a 1,000 MB file occupy (before replication)?

story.title: Adding a cache server without a meltdown

scenes.text: A web site spreads its cache keys over 3 servers. The team adds a 4th for Diwali sales.
With naive hashing nearly every key moves and the cache empties. Consistent hashing moves only a fraction.

steps.title: Ring
steps.body: Hash both **nodes** and **keys** onto the same circular space (e.g. 0 to 2^32 - 1). A key is stored on the **first node clockwise** from its position (its successor). Adding or removing a node only affects the keys between that node and its predecessor: on average **K/N** keys move (K keys, N nodes).

steps.title: Virtual nodes
steps.body: Each physical server is placed at many points on the ring (e.g. 100-200 virtual nodes). This evens out load, and a failed node's keys spread over many neighbours. Used in Dynamo, Cassandra, memcached clients and CDNs; Chord uses the idea for peer-to-peer lookup in O(log N) hops with finger tables.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body: Ring 0-99, nodes at 10, 40, 70. Key 55 -> next node >= 55 = 70. Key 95 -> wraps around to 10. Key 10 -> 10. Add a node at 60: only keys in (40,60] (previously on 70) move to 60.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the wrap-around.
- Using too few virtual nodes: unbalanced load, hot spots.

scenes.text: Clerk 1 reads a balance, Clerk 2 writes a new one, Clerk 1 then writes his own. The final balance silently erases clerk 2's work (lost update).
The schedule is not equivalent to any serial order of the two transactions.

steps.title: ACID
steps.body: **Atomicity**, **Consistency** (application invariants), **Isolation**, **Durability**. A schedule is **serializable** if equivalent to some serial execution. **Conflict serializable** if it can be turned into a serial one by swapping non-conflicting operations. Two operations conflict if they are on the same item, by different transactions and at least one is a write.

steps.title: Precedence graph test
steps.body: Draw a node for each transaction and an edge Ti -> Tj when an operation of Ti conflicts with and precedes an operation of Tj. The schedule is conflict serializable **iff the graph has no cycle**.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body: Schedule r1(x) w2(x) w1(x): r1 before w2 gives T1 -> T2; w2 before w1 gives T2 -> T1. Cycle, so **not serializable**.

steps.title: Concurrency control
steps.body: **Two-phase locking (2PL)**: acquire all locks before releasing any (growing then shrinking phase); strict 2PL holds write locks to commit. Guarantees serializability but can deadlock. **Timestamp ordering** and **optimistic (OCC)** and **MVCC** (snapshot isolation) avoid blocking readers. Across services without 2PC use the **saga** pattern: a chain of local transactions with compensating actions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing 'serial' (one at a time) with 'serializable' (equivalent to one at a time).
- Believing snapshot isolation is serializable: write skew is possible.

lessons.title: Lab: Partitioning (sharding) and why mod-N hashing hurts

scenes.text: A table of 500 million orders no longer fits one server. The team shards it across 4 databases using order_id mod 4.
Adding a 5th shard remaps almost every row. A painful migration.

steps.title: Strategies
steps.body:
- **Range partitioning**: key ranges per shard (good for range scans; hot spots with sequential keys like timestamps).
- **Hash partitioning**: hash(key) mod N (even spread; poor range scans; resharding cost).
- **Directory/lookup**: a table maps keys to shards (flexible, extra hop).
- **Consistent hashing** with virtual nodes; **fixed number of many partitions** assigned to nodes (Kafka, Elasticsearch, Cassandra token ranges).
Pick a key with high cardinality and even access; avoid cross-shard joins and transactions.

steps.title: Solved: mod-N reshuffle
steps.body: Keys 0..19, going from N = 4 to N = 5 shards. Key k stays only if k mod 4 = k mod 5: that holds for k = 0, 1, 2, 3 only. So **16 of 20 keys (80%) move**. With consistent hashing only about 1/5 = 20% would move.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sharding by a low-cardinality key (country): one huge shard.
- Forgetting hot keys (a celebrity user) that overload one shard regardless of hashing.

scenes.text: Nisha has the distributed systems exam tomorrow.

steps.title: Models and availability
steps.body:
- Series A = A1.A2; parallel A = 1 - (1-A1)(1-A2).
- Amdahl S = 1/((1-p) + p/N); max speedup 1/(1-p).
- Fallacies: network reliable, latency zero, bandwidth infinite, secure, topology fixed, one admin, transport cost zero, homogeneous.

steps.title: Time and ordering
steps.body:
- Cristian: T = T_server + RTT/2.
- Berkeley: send adjustments = average - own difference.
- Lamport: local/send C += 1; receive C = max(C, ts) + 1.
- Vector: receive = elementwise max then own entry + 1; V < W iff all <= and not equal.

steps.title: Coordination and consensus
steps.body:
- Mutual exclusion messages: centralised 3; Ricart-Agrawala 2(N-1); token ring 1 to N-1.
- Bully: highest live id wins; ring election about 2N messages.
- 2PC: 4 messages per participant; blocks if coordinator fails.
- Majority = floor(N/2)+1; crash tolerance N = 2f+1; Byzantine N = 3f+1.
- Raft commit index = (n+1)/2-th largest match index (majority).

steps.title: Replication and storage
steps.body:
- Quorum: R + W > N and W > N/2.
- CAP: during a partition choose C or A; PACELC adds latency vs consistency.
- G-Counter merge = element-wise max.
- HDFS: 128 MB blocks, replication 3. Consistent hashing moves ~K/N keys; mod-N moves most.
